div.head: 'WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: 'WOMEN'S CHAT.

Earthquake Terrors.—Minor earthquakes we are told are not uncommon in the British Isles, but happily they are not often noticable. Our ancestors however, used to indulge in earthquake panics, and if we had many severe shocks as the recent one in Wales, which caused considerable damage of the smaller kind, we ' should soon begin to live in terror of thern.There was a great scare in London after the earthquake in 1750, which Sir Isaac Newton attributed to dry weather, and ; predicted another unless rain fell. In consequencej great numbers of people left London for the country, and many who remained prepared warm clothing, and , made arrangements for sleeping out of doors. There eras another panic in 1755, when the earthquake which destroyed Lisbon occurred, and was felt throughout the western hemisphere. The fact that that distur- ! bane extended right across the Altantic does not help: the theory that earthquakes are influeneed by conditions of the local rainfall. Society Conversation.—Lady Hugh Bell, who pre- ' sided at the seventeenth annual Women Writers' Dinner, is a well-known author of plays, stories, and books for children, and has written several very charming novels. She had much to say on the subject of Society slang, and general conversation and seemed to agree with the prevalent opinion that this is of a lower standard than was the case in the mid-Victorian period. People seem now to talk of little else than their amusements, health, and the latest "cures," and when they have said a little about the theatres, holidays, and watering places, they go bock to the subject of their diseases. It has been suagested that hostesses should place on their menu cards, all topics of conversation that are not to be dis- cussed, during dinner, but it is to be feared that in that case it would often he reduced to almost a dumb show. The perfect dinner-table talker of former times would now be voted tiresome and prosy, and the most appreci- ated seem to be the people who are smart in the slang and jargon of the day: As a rule they hit upon one word, or short ungrammatical sentence, which, for the time being becomes the fashion. Everything that is not pleasant is" rot "and everyone who is not agreeable is a rotter." Just now there seems to be a difficnity in discovering a successor to "absolutely " which has long been the favourite tag amongst so-called smart Society. Deadening the Noise of the Trafflc.—Several of ;he great London hostesses have hit upon the device of • having the roadway covered with straw or moss litter on their entertainment nights in order to enjoy open windows and deadeq the noise of the traffic. Some of • the stately mansions suffer as much in this respect as the dwellings of the more humble classes, and leading artistes and vocalists object to appear in drawing rooms where outside noise wilt somewhat mar the effect of their performance. Hence the resort to the straw,which instead of being taken—as it invariably is, as evidence of a serious case of illness, may only morn that some other great lady is giving a reception and music, or some other entertainment. Roof Gardens.—ln the hot weather the Londoner sighs in vain for the at frisco meals beloved by the Parisians, and there are no roof gardens in the Metropolis as in New York where the people resort for open-air refreshments and entertainment in the summer time. In America, the cult of the roof garden has been carried to a fine art, and at one of these sky-scraper boweries in New York, there is the exact counterpart of a farm- yard, with cows, geese, fowls, and everything in keeping. London is too sooty for such artificial rnralism, and no doubt it is the dirt and smoke which would be ruinous to summer frocks that is the drawback to the establish- ment of the fashionable roof garden, as it is seen in 'New York. So far the only attempts in London to turn roof leads to account have been those on working , class blocks, where they are railed in, and serve as a drying-ground for the washing. The London Shops.—London is shortly to have a mammoth drapery business on the lines of an American dry-goods store. Many Americana have cherished the ambition of establishing a vast business in "the biggest city in the world," Rad it is now announced that Mr. H. G. Selfridge is to carry it out. He was a partner with the late Mr. Marshall Field the founder of the huge store in Chicago which ranks as one of the wonders of • the world. Compared with it, the famous Bon Marche and the Louvre in Paris are small concerns, although! the latter far exceed in size any „of the London shops. Whether the latter have anything to learu from , American methods is however very doubtfuk They may not be quite so large, buttin all other respects they will compare favourably with the retail establishments of any of the great capitals of the world. Concerning Ospreys.—lt would seem as though nothing could be said to shame us out of wearing ospreys, for these beautiful plumes still continue to decorate {?) the heads, and headgear of fashionable women. We have flowers innumerable. to choose from, natural and unnatural : ostrich plumes in every known. • size and colour ; and fruit so realistic that if it were , placed upon the table insteau of in our hats and toques, few of us would detect that it is not likely to Drove ' as good to eat as it is to look at. The new flower aigrettes are exceedingly graceful and pretty, and so also are the sheaves of barley, which have almost es light an effect as the osprey itself. Yet immbers of women persist in passing all these pretty and innocent trimmings by. to seize upon the beautiful plume which entails so much cruelty and suffering, both to the parent birds and their young. The wearer of the osprey can no longer—after all that has been said and written upon the subject, plead ignorance of how and when ospreys are obtained, and if hostessea would but follow in the footsteps of her Majesty the Queen, the Princess of Wales, and a few of oar great ladies, and cause it to be known that they obient to receive guests who permit these plumes to find a place in their hats or on their heala, much might he done to stamp out a mode that is orrelv a disgrace to,civilised women. A Familiar Fabric.—Our old friend foulard, like navy

blue serge. is always With us, and this year the only difference lies in the abolition of the spot, and the Japanese curly-hews, and the undisputed reign of the large white lozenge or diamond. Few materials wear and clean better than foulard, and when trimmed with a little good lace, a foulard frock can well hold its own on all save quite dressy occasions. New Colours.—The latest colour is "hortensia pink," which by the way is more inclined to take a manve,tban a pink shade. This particular colour is having an , immense vogue in Paris, especially when " batiste de toile,"and mousseline de soie are the fabrics fixed upon. So far this has been a blue, a pale blue summer with us, but modistes are now- bringing forward the most exquisite shades of mauve and heliotrope, and the new " hortensia pink." _

div.head: OUT-DOOR MUSIC.
div.p: OUT-DOOR MUSIC.

Music entertains, comforts,thrillsjust as much during the long days and twilight evenings of summer as in the dreary cheerlessness of winter. When the summer shadows are lengthening in the cool of the day, when man's work is none and the air is filled with the fragrance of flowers and the evening songs of birds,then it is that sweet music harmonizes most perfectly with the mood of man and nature. A form of summer pleasure that is ever becoming more popular is the enjoyment on the lawn, in the quiet country, on the boating excursion, of vocal and instrumental music by the grapho-phone. After it becomes too dark for tennis, young people gather •to be entertained by band and orchestra, and to join in singing favourite and comic songs under the leadership of the grapho-phone. The picnic and summer camp are enlivened by the presence of this versatile and accomplishe4 entertainer. Columbia grapho-phones and, recotds stiNable for out door use are to be had in both disc and cylinder styles. Full information with lists of selections will be s.nt to all who write for "Price Book 20" to the Columbia Phonograph Co., General, 89, Great Eastern-street London, E.C.
w CO-OPERATIVE STAFF PICNIC.

The annual picnic of the steff of Earlestown Co-operative Society took place on Wednesday last week, Blackpool being the rendezvous. Between 70 and SO travelled by the 5.55 and 8.45 trains, special carriages being attached to the former. Rain fell heavily in the early morning, but by the time Preston was reached the dark clon-is gave way to sunshine and the remainder of the day was beautifully fine. Blackpool was reached at 9.14 and then the party breakfasted and separated for the day in search of pleasure and amusement, not a difficult task in Blackpool. After spending a very enjoyable day the visitors returned by the two evening trains, a special train being provided at Wigan to avoid a long wait ia connections. Each member of the staff was given a day's holiday and 7s. 6d. towards the necessary expenses. Mr. A. Onions (secretary) made the Arrangements.

WOMAN'S REALM.

grown muscle, yet upon his temples was a touch of snow;_ and though many had loved him with wakened passion, this, indeed, was the first time a woman arA .4 child in one greeted him as the ye unfruitful earth, in ancient myth and fable, hailed the advent of Apollo. He was infinitely touched and very grateful; not one unhappy thought, akin to a sneer, bade him note with conceit how she had given him a bounty that he had not asked. Who, indeed, knew that he had not asked for it subtly, and unknown even to himself, since he saw now how desirable, how fit a mate she was for him? To work for his advantage had been her pleaeure, 'ter own sweet task. She had •risked much and achieved much ; she had given him his desire. And yet, through it and in it all ran a thread, not of

irony, but of the humour sometimes happily spp!trent in the yeti nature of things. Her mingled daring and cowardice, her innocence and sweet cunning, her pride, her fears, her , audacious con- tempt for godlike regulations, and her victorious attack upon those who wielded them, chewed her in so sweet and mingled a light that Richard smiled, and then laughed with a great shout of laughter. Sach laughter had not been his for years; it cleared his very soul of bitterness. He felt so like a youth again that a grey s hair was now an accident, and no premeditated insult of Time. He regarded his enemies with humorous yet lofty contempt; audacious magic had rolled them in the dirt; prone and supine in all the various attitudes of ludicrous disaster they invited pitying comment. Sir Dan was now no man of iron, a bold push chewed him lath and plaster; even the great Chief himself was very human. What would he not have given to have overheard her talk.with Graham. The very notion was stupendous. He laughed again, and, going to the Army and Navy Club, wrote letters to the Deputy Adjutant-General, to Colonel Briggs, and to Billy. He told Wills nothing more would be heard of the telegram, and promised him a personal explanation when he returned. "That will intrigue him, and keep me in his mind," said. Richard. And to dear old Briggs he sent personal news concerning some commissions he had undertaken-for him; adding that all was well with him, and that he would be hack inside six months. He told Billy, now so much more to him than a newly-joined subaltern, that he hoped soon to have the pleasure of making his sister's acquaintance. "They say she is a great beauty. me that." And then he sat dreaming in an armchair, wondering if he should ask her to marry him at once. Ana would she ? What about her people, and the tight and shining dragon of a mother ? And 'would Sir Dan tell Mn. Gretton ? Poor, poor Madge! What a time she would have if he did. Richard was half inclined to see him again, and request him to be good enough to say nothing about it. And yet, of course, that would be useless at the best. It Might even do harm. Thank Heaven, Madge knew where to find him if he was wanted.
You never told

And even as the lover thought of Madge, she, the beloved, was hiddeil in her bedroom, and went red and pale by turns. She had been late for lunch, which led to lamentation; she was talked at through the soup and cutlets till she was ready to scream. Then in the afternoon Sir Dan came in. Madge looked over the banisters and saw him at his worst. He was not now the debonair soldier

who 'carries his years as a grenadier carries a cane; he was old and ugly and fierce; a ruffled cockatoo of screaming war. He demanded Mrs. Gretton peremptorily with a drum-head court-martial air, and, pacing the drawing-room till she came, fired off subdued bad language. "Dear Sir Dan; so glad to see you again. You come far too seldom," cried Mrs. Gretton, languidly. "Your dear daughter comes in often; we a3k her why she never brings you. Now, why don't you come? div.head: DRESS-FASMON-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASMON-HOME.
THE PRINCEES OF MONACO.

As much at home in London as in Paris is the clever and cultivated Princess of Monaco—in- deed, since her second marriage she has always had an English lady-in-waiting, and when host4ss of the splendid old castle in the princi- pality from which her liusband takes his title she was always specially kindly in her reception of British visitors. Most people are aware that the Princess was related to the great poet Heine; fewer know that she is half-American by birth. As Mlle. Alice Heine, she was one of the greatest of Parisian heiresses, and in earliest youth she became the wife of the_ late Due de Richelieu. Her husband died -prematurely, and for nine years she was one of the most beautiful and courted of widows in .the great cosmopolitan world. Then, in the October of 1839, she became the wife of the then heir-apparent of the Prince of Monaco.

div.head: PRETTY DRESS.
div.p: A PRETTY DRESS.

In our sketch is sheWn a pretty dress which would be suitable to be copied in any thin mate- rial. It is made in the Princess style, and the material is closely gauged about the waist, the gauging being continued about three inches below the waist. The gathered flounce is put on with a heading of gauging, and is finished at the hem with three large tucks. The material above the elbow is simply/gathered on to a small round yoke composed of several rows of Valenciennes

lace. The sleeves are short, drawn in above the elbow by gauging, and finished with two full frills. pver the dress a dainty lace bolero is worn, composed of piece lace, and edged with a band of insertion, which hangs in two stole ends down the front. POLITICAL HOSTESSES' DILEMMA.

Radical entertaintnents of a private character are a distinct failure this season. Primarily, says Vanity Fair, the parties within the party object to mixing. They will not wear the same manners nor the same clothes, and al'e for shak- ing off the dast of unwilling proximity from dis- similar boots. Hostesses,, brilliant in resource though they be, are afraid to engage anything so risque as a pierrot troupe for fear of com- plicating some aspect of social reforro, or to give peaches in June lest they bring a reminder of the bitter fruit of extravagance rattling about their heads. ; Diplomacy is vain when a Labour Member discovers that an absent-minded Peer has made away with his hat.

div.head: COLONIAL THREAT.
div.p: A COLONIAL THREAT.

The Colonial wife is not to be trifled with. When her husband goes "up country" and neg- lects to return within a fair and reasonable time she simply advertises for him: Here is a recent advertisement from an Australian paper: "If my husband, A. 8., does not answer this adver- tisement in three weeks. I intend to get \ mar- ried.—(Signed) C.D."

div.head: CHARMING MODEL.
div.p: CHARMING MODEL.

Rather a charming model, says the Ladies' Field, is a combination of the Princess and corselet styles, swathed round the figure over an entire blouse of cornflower-blue and brown tulle, worn with a hat of this uncommon inixture. The craze for mixing coloured tulles on frocks is in- creasing, but it will probably be only the fashion of the hour; it is rather a pretty one, and an effective way of lightening some of our last year's gowns.

div.head: DAINTY PELERINE.
div.p: A DAINTY PELERINE.
Dainty little pelerines of chiffon or silk have become quite an important feature of our sum- mer attire. As a general rule, they are (worn in

conjunction with fluffy light frocks of main, and very charming, and effective addition., to the toilet they make. The particular example pic- tured in our sketch is specially pretty and be- coming. , It is fashioned of white silk patterned

with a lovely chine design of pale pink roses, blue, forget-rue-note, and green leaves. The pelerine is arranged in crossover form, and is cut considerably wider on the shoulders. The silk is draped round the figure in most becoming fashion, crossed back and front, and fastened in front with long hanging ends. Double frills of taffetas border the lower edge, which frills develop on the shoulders into a fluffy cascade of five or six little flounces.

div.head: HINTS FOR PICNIC LUNCHES.
div.p: HINTS FOR PICNIC LUNCHES.

As the success of a picnic lunch of course de., ponds greatly on the cateful packing of the food, a few hints may be !iseful to the novice, says P.T.O. The meat, poultry, and similar dishes should be folded in greased paper, and every- thing which is likely to be crushed, such as galantines or fish, should be packed in a card- board box. Salad materials travel best if they are wrapped in a damp ,cloth and put in a tin. All liquids, milk, cream, salad dressing and the like, must be put in bottles, and be well corked. Butter goes best in jam pots. French pastry, tartlets. and the like should be arranged in layers in a tin, with paper between each. Jellies i may go to the picnic n their moulds. Crockery, cutlery, silver, &c., will, of course, be packed in separate hampers or cases, and the systematic housewife will not forget to have each parcel labelled. It is not amusing, for instance, to have to open all the packages in a wild chase ror the tablecloth, which is needed first. Take as much, fruit as possible. It is always decora- tive as well as popular.

"I did not dare answer it. I was afraid of getting you into trouble." "It was kind of you to think of it." She looked at him for one swift moment. "But you are in trouble now?" Richard smiled. "Oh, it's nothing, nothing really. And I had my chance. Thanks to some good friend of mine." Madge looked up anxiously. "Oh, but was it a friend?" "Yes, yes," said Richard, "whatever happens. But who was my friend, Margaret?" Her own name was sweet to her ears-then, for all her mother's formal use of it. "How should I know?" she cried, softly. "But you do know." "No, no. Yes." "Who's he?" asked Blundell, with pleasing acidity. "I don't know him, but he did very well in Burmah," said Madge, "and got nothing after all." "Oh!" cried Richard. CHAPTER XVII.

Richard Blundell, when he saw her drive away, and beheld her at once so happy and so mournful,' wondered at the ways of the gods and their gifts to men. What virtue, what noble apparel of mind or of body,- had won this fair creature for him. What strange seduction of eyo or speech, enduring yet with his remaining youth, had taken this sweet child captive? Conscious though he was of mighty strength, concealed rather in nerve than in over-
"Sh7Fan't 'ad* hifn, MO,It sne Goes, what WC. she go about ? Tell me, ten me I " And Sir Dan did tell her the whole story, so far as he knew it.
"Oh, wretched, impulsive, foolish, foolish child," cried Mrs. Gretton. "She may befoolish. But she is no-fool," said Sir Dan, bitterly, "unless she's been made one by this fellow." _ _ _

Mrs. Gretton collapsed on the cushions add wept. She asked Heaven, as usual in all emergencies, why she had ever been born, why she had ever married, why she had not died an early death, ere disaster came upon her. Would dear, kind Sir Daniel tell her what to do? Would he promise to say nothing to anybody ?, Would he put Blundell somewhere in the foreground of the battle, and have him killed immediately before worse came of it ? Unless he promised that, there was nothing for her but death. "With a girl of her wild spirit of unseemly independence, there is nothing for it but to marry her at once. Mr. Maitland is deeply in love with her; thank Heaven for that." "She'll never marry Bobby Maitland," said Sir Dan, scornfully. "She shall," cried/her mother, with unartificial emphasis. "I'll see that she does. You must send this Blundell away, Sir Dan, for she must not math him. WA ran leave nothing to chance." If Madge had not bitterly wounded Sir Dan's vanity he might have said it was no business of his. "But I can't send him away." "Then what is the good of your being the Adjutant-General? " sobbed Mrs. Gretton. thoug.ht you could do nearly everything." "Then you were wrong in thinking so," said Si] Dan, curtly. '

He paceil up and down the room. "Do you really believe there is any chance of hcl marrying young Maitland if Blundell was got out of the way ? " "Of course there is," said Mrs. Gretton, whc was always full of hope even after the most disastrous defeat. Like the Afghans, who only sing songs celebrating their victories over the Sirkar, she was oblivious of past reverses. "Then I'll think it over and see if something can be done. But I'd advise you not to drive her tc desperation. You see the sort of girl she is."

ft was bitter humiliation for 'Mrs. Gretton to I swallow advice concerning her daughter; especially as she had a chance of taking her at a monstrous disadvantage, but she did swallow it withyt moan. "It's so good of you to have treated her merci- fully. Oh, the shame of it; oh, the shame of it!" And Sir Dan departed, leaving Mrs. Gretton groaning on the sofa, for onde with a real attack of indigestion. It was a blessed consolation to her in trouble, for lately she had been so intolerably well that she had quarrelled with a doctor indis- creet enough to remark that she looked first-rate. I Had it not been a commonplace among West End physicians that Mrs. Gretton could not be relied on as a faithful patient, this particular one might have regretted her guineas. But now she felt really unwell; she had a pain, a most distinct pain. And it was due to Margaret. She rang the bell, and commanded Margaret's appearance. • For once Margaret was really afraid of her mother,. and 'declined the combat.

• "Miss Margaret says she has a headache, and is lying down, ma'am," said Mrs. Gretton's messenger. So Mrs. Gretton sent for a new doctor, one she had heard spoken of nicely at afternoon teas, and ,described her distinct pain to sympathetic ears. She made up her mind during the evening as to the course it was desirable to take with Margaret; and had her temper permitted her to stick to it her plan was not without its merits. She would sacrifice herself and return to the country, where Margaret would find it difficult to get into mischief. While there was any danger of her meeting this absurd hero of hers in the country she-would remain. Sir Dan, brute as he was, shewed a certain' sense of Margaret's deficiencies in thinking she would bear justifiable rebuke badly. She therefore determined to avoid rebuking her for a time. Her health would not permit her to entertain much. She would ask Robert Maitland down for Christmas. Mrs. • Gretton instinctivelv felt she could make Gfetton House so infinitely -dull that even Bobby Maitland would be a relief.

And during the night it occurred to Mrs. Gretton that her duty demanded an inspection of Margaret's room. She had been remiss in proper surveillance. What did the girl know of this Blundell? How very unfortunate it was that, he should have become intimate with Billy. Imagine Mr. Gretten meeting him in town and asking him to diner! "It is the thing the fool would do," criecrAmelia as she fell asleep. She woke after one of her bad nights. She had only slept eight solid hours. With her eyes firmly fixed on Duty she rose at half-past nine, to the astonishment of the household, and after breakfast went to Margaret's room. For the girl always rode with her father in the Row early in the morning whenever they were in town, summer or winter. Her mother had no difficulty in discovering the whereabouts of Madge's particular treasures. For since she had been tall enough to reach the top right-hand drawer of a certain old mahogany chest of drawers everything precious had been deposited there. And Madge's lock gave way to Mrs. Gretton's keys on the third try. In the drawer was one battered doll, which, sleeping under her pillows for many years, had been a bed fetish for Madge. A scrap-bobk con- tamed pictures _pictures mostly of military life, in which many Generals smoked short pipes given them by Billy, when, with the ruthless brutality of a boy, he outraged every susceptibility of his sister by doinglyhat his mother did now. A packet of news- paper cuttings tied with ribbon lay on top of a hymn-book. under which was a copy of "Jane Eyre." Such juxtaposition was blasphemy to Mrs. Gretton ; she could scarcely restrain herself from parting the dreadful opposites. Then came "Signalling Instructions," and a book on ciphers. Mrs. Gretton groaned. At the back of the drawer, under a silk scarf, was a bundle of photographs. Nay, there were two bundles. Mrs. Gretton lifted them with eager fingers, and found beneath them again an old ° journal of the proceedings of the Geographical Society, and an "Arabic Grammar for Beginners," by Captain Richard Blundell! "I thought si,s much," said Mrs. Gretton, triumphantly, as she picked it up between finger and thumb.

In the journal she found a report of a lecture on t? journey through Somaliland by the same ruffian. She sorted out the photographs. Napoleon was on the top, and, regardless of history and her patriotism, Wellington underneath. "Humph," said Mrs. Gretton, who regarded Napoleon as Anti-Christ and a confounder of noble homes and royalty.- Then she • saw Wolfe, and a cut-out likeness of Sir John Moore. She dropped them and picked up Clive and Warren Hastings. Nicholson, of Punjab, confronted her. Then Beresford, and Wolseley, and Lord Aoberts, and a photograph of an ancient coin supposed to bear Hannibal upon it. Madge evidently mixed her heroes. Mrs. Gretton put them together again and tied them up. She loosened the ribbon of the second bundle, 'and 'found Billy there, and Mr. Gretton., and two new photographs unknown. One was of a squat, ugly man, marked in pencil "Renshaw" ; and the other was a curious, hard, striking face of a man of thirty-one or twos "Who's this, I wonder?" said Mrs. Gretton. "Why, it must be someone I know." She puzzled over it. "If I know it—wily, it can't be this Blundell. And I'm sure I've seen him somewhert."
She racked her mind to remember, and grew quite absorbed in the struggle. "Why," she cried at last, in triumph, "it's that Portughese at Chillon." She heard a little click behind her.

_ "No, mother, irs Captain Blundell," said Madge. "You atrociously wicked girl! How dare you frighten me?" gasped Mrs. Gretton, utterly losing her dignity. "Oh, how dare you look in my drawer ? " cried Madge. "Oh, how dare you, how dare you!"

"bon't you dare say. 'dare' to me," answered her mother, dropping the red-hot photograph, which Madge instantly picked up. "You wretched girl, you deceitful, disgraceful child, what have you done ? " Madge's lip trembled. "I don't care," she cried ; "and I'd do it again." "Do what ? " "It," said Madge, with a gulp, as she swallowed a sob.
She would not cry now. No one but Richard should ever make her cry again. And if he wasn't angry and Lord Graham had laughed, what did it matter ?

"Yesterday afternoon Sir Daniel Fielding came to see me,''bsaid her mother, in a sepulchral voice, as she recovered herself. "Horrible old Sir Dan. I hate him," cried Madge. whitely. "And what did he tell me, oh, what did he tell

—no. I do not, said rbradje, with a curious touch of weariness in her voice.

It jarred on her mother, for it suggested that the girl was really grown up and not a child any longer. "How am I to speak to her ? " demanded Mrs. Gretton, with uplifted hands. "How am I to bring her to a sense, a proper sense, of what she has done? Oh, lam an unhappy woman I" She recalled that distinct pain of yesterday. "She makes me ill. I might die in agony, rolling on the floor, and what would she care? I can conceive my thankless child rejoicing at having me removed from her path. Give me that photograph, Margaret." "I won't," said Madge, stubbornly; and to prevent its being wrenched from her she put it in her pocket. ,"How did you come by it, girl ?" "I bought it." "Ah I And when ? "
Madge did not answer, and suddenly .light dawned on Mrs. Gretton.

"Good Heavens! Is this Blundell the man you dared to have lunch with on a mountain?" "Yes, it is," said Madge, sitting down on the edge of her bed. "Stand up. How dare you sit down 1" cried her mother.

But Madue did not move."iwon't " cried Madge, "and it was Captain Blundell I was With that day. And he was very nice and kind. And if old Sir Dan did tell you I don't care a bit, and tell it to father myself." "Oh," said Mrs. Gretton, weakly, "how did you venture to let me think he was a Portuguese? " "Well, when I said he wasn't you talked me down," replied Madge. "And when I said he had, moustaches like a walrus you were quite angry, because you seethed to like him." Mrs. Graton snorted.

- "I seemed to like him? L seemed to like him ?' And fot his sake, for this wretch's sake, you have committed crimes. Yes, your father must be told. It will serve him sight. We will go back to Gretton House at once. I must do my duty, if I die. 11l as I'am I will take you out of London away from danger. A daughter of mine to have acted so ! I am punished indeed for anything I may have done in my unhappy life. Oh, you dreadful and disgraceful chila 1" Madge jumped up with blazing eyes. "I won't be called disgraceful, for I'm not. And your Sir Dan is a wicked, horrid old man! I know Miss F elding thinks he is. • And Lord Graham didn't think I was a disgrace. If he did would he have laughed?" "Lord Gtaham laughed? You tell me he laughed ? I don't believe be would have laughed!" cried her mother. "And if he did he's not • fit to :be Commander-in-Chief. But I will speak to you no more. Get ready to go back to the country. Pack now Heaven be merciful to me, a most unhappy woman!"
(To be continued.)

div.head: LIFE ALMOST UNBEARABLE.
div.p: LIFE ALMOST UNBEARABLE.
Butler's Constant Suffering from Stomach Troubles Ended by Bile Beans.

"One half the world doesn't know how the other lives." This ancient adage has been strikingly exempli- fied in the experience of Mr. Herbert Beattie, of 74, Primrose Road, Beckett. Street, Leeds. Mr. Beattie is a butler at Rawdon College, fnear Leeds. He suffered severely for three years from gastric catarrh and indiges- tion.

"I was obliged to stick to my duties and put as good a face on the matter as I could,"he told a local report&- " Vor three years my life was one constant misery. My stomach was so sore and weak that I couldn't eat any solid food. Always after s meal, no matter how light. I suffered from nausea. Often I was doubled up wit!' stomach pain, and racked with acute headaches. One inormng I got up in such pain that I didn't really know sant I was doing. Just as I was abbut to serve breakfast, I oollapied and fell with my hands the fire. I was lifted out and carried to bed, where 1 remained for several days. Though it scarely sounds credible, it is Quite true that for a long time I didn't ncifice that my hand was burned, so severe were the pains from the indigestion. "I paid p_oands in doctors' bills, and attendeds

Ileedas: dispensary for a time, but never obtained the benefit. The doctors told me I was suffering ir°'" gastric catarrh and indigestion. I really thought I should have to give my work up,as I was getting worse. Then I tried Bile Beans. From that time I began to get better, and now I arn as well in health as ever I Was." NEW CONTINENTAL CORRIDOR VESTIBULED EXPRESS. .

For the convenience of travellers from Scotland, the Northern and Midland counties of England by Harwich Route to the Continent, the Great Eastern Railway Company will place a new and improved type of train on the service between Lincoln and Parkeston Quay, Harwich, on and from July 2nd. The train is corridor throughout, allowing Passengers to walk from end to end. .Dining and breakfast cars are provided so that dassengers can dine or take refreshments, h la carte, on the up journey, and table d'hôte breakfast on the down journey on their return to England. The trein is lighted throughout by electricity, and is provided for the winter months with a system of steam 'heating, which can be regulated by passengers in each carriage. Passengers from Manchester by the Great Central Railway will travel in a through corridor coach to Lincoln station where the carriage will be attached to the train, allowing passengers to join the dining cars. In the reverse direction the through coach will run to Man- chester and the service tO Manchester will ~be accelerated.

THE INFIRMARY, EXTENSION. THE CORPORATION GIVE A DONATION? INTERESTING DISCUSSION. Finance and Estate Committee reported that considered an application from the Infirmary ittee for a donation towards the extension fund. 3 resolved "That as the Corporation have no ltovhich could properly be given as a donation for °ova purpose, and as they are advised that they t otherwise legally grant a donation, this corn- regret that they are unable to make any recom-

mendation. The only course open for the Corporation to enable them to make the grant would be by obtain- ing Parliamentary powers to do so." Alderman BENNETT, in moving the adoption of the minutes. said they all regretted they were not able to give a donation to the Infirmary. It only, emphasized what had long been strongly impressed upon him, and that was that infirmaries, which were of such immense moment to the welfare of a town like Warrington, ought to be provided by Corporations and be under Corporation coL.trol. It was absurd that for an institution which was absolutely necessary, they should have to strain every nerve and make herculean efforts to support it. Under the present system the generous were mulcted for the sake of the mean. If the infirmaries were under the control of Corporations then everybody would have to pay a fair share. Councillor PEIIBEICTON : Hear. hear. Counoillor FULTON SMITH seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor WRIGHT moved an amendment that the minute relating to the Infirmary/ be referred back for further consideration. He considered the resolution was contradictory and misleading, and showed a dis- tinct spirit ef unwillingness on the part of the com- mittee to make a recommednation to the Council. There was a way and means whereby a grant could, be made. In March last, the Liverpool Finance Com- mittee made a recommendation, and it was passed by the Council by 38 votes to 18. that in the next applica- tion to Parliament there should be included power to contribute £5,000 towards the rebuilding of the Children's Infirmary in Myrtle-street. If Liver- pool could make that recommendation, it was within the power of Wei ring ton to make one. He waa not going to advocate, that they should contribute £50,000, but seeing that a private employer (Mr. Long), had given £l,OO0— and he (Councillor Wright) was informed that other employers were going to make gifts of £l.ooo—the Cor- porationas being the largest employers of labour, might make a ,grant of £2,000, which would be as dttle as they could do. It was a downright shame in a civilized and so-called Christian land that the State found hundreds of millions of pounds to destroy life and property, and yet up to the present had not seen its way to supply funds to support institutions whose objects were to save life and repair injuries. It was an 'abominable shame that the Warrington Infirmary should have to depend solely upon the charitable donations and collections derived from gorgeous displays of tinsel and paper. He asked the Council to give a little hnmane consideration to the application, and , treat it with common-sense, and rob the resolution 'of superfluous officialism. The MAYOR : You cannot expect the Finance Com- mittee to give money if they have none. The Liverpool Committee have private funds. WRIGH, : They have no such funds. The MAYOR: Well, they have to go to Parliament. Councillor WRIGHT: That is what they have done i and what our Finance Committee suggests s the only way to get money. ' Councillor Dr. JOSEPH seconded the amendment. He said so much cold 'water had been thrown on this appli- cation that he candidly admitted he had not much hope for it. It was a very proper application to be con- sidered without prejudice. From his experience of past applications, there had been an undue and improper amount of prejudice against them. He was very sorry to see tbe apathy on this matter, and, in some quarters, decided opposition to it. Councillor WiratrssoN said the Infirmary had always had his deepest sympathy. He did not know whether he was one of the cold water gentlemen "referred to because he bappened to tackle this matter in rather a practical and not too sympathetic spirit. When £250 i and £5OO was proposed n the General Purposes Com- mittee, he (Councillor Wilkinson) said it was little enough for Warrington to provide £l,OOO, but before he gave his vote he wanted to know what representa- tion the Council was going to have on the Infirmary Board. He (Councillor Wilkinson) had given hundreds of hours to the gorgeous displays of tinsel and paper, and had used his purse to make their carnivals a success He had done his duty, and hoped the gentlemen who had spoken had done as much. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH: Whom do you mean? Councillor WILKINSON : There are only two of you. (Laughter.) Councillor Dr. JOSEPH: I have done as much as you have. You are not the only man who does any- thing. Councillor WiratnesoN : I claim I have done as much for that institution as any gentleman in the borough, barring the late Alderman Roberts. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH : Question. Councillor WILKINSON: I have heard a good many talkers. _ .

I Alderman TIN.NION seconded, and said that th\33, all felt that not only had the tows lost an able and earnest Worker, and a willing one, but they had each lost a Personal friend. Alderman Roberts was one who did 511 he could for the betterment of the people of the I,°.wn• (Hear, hear.) His genial good nature endesred "Ito to all of them. "Mile he rendered very valuable 4rvice as a member of the Corporation, the greatest Zc'rk he did, and which would stand out more promi- tntly than anything else, was that in connection with C 4 Infirmary, and they all regretted that he had not 111 to see the completion, of the extension of that titution. (Rear, hear.) th2°,oncillor PEMBERTON in supporting characterized l ate Alderman Roberts as "one of nature's noble- He did not think there was ever a member of Council who was straighter, more honest, or who veoged bettSr. for the ratepayers. Conncillor Dr. JOSEPH : Well, tell the truth. Councillor WILKINSON said he had been willing all along to give his vote towards a handsome donation, but the Council had no funds or powers at present. He suggested they should acoept the minutes, and let some gentleman bring forward a resolution to go to Parlia- ment for powers to make the Infirmary a donation. Councillor PEIMRTON said Councillor Wilkinson's remarks made him think that be (Councillor Wilkinson) knew very little about the Infirmary. Dr. Joseph had given his professional services to the Infirmary free which was equivalent and sometimes more than equiva- lent to money. The question was whether it would be expedient for the Town Council to go to Parliament for powers, because it was possible that the cost would be as much as they would give to the Infirmary. The MAYOR.: Quite right. Councillor PEMBERTON That does not say we can- not do it some way. I think it would be better if the matter was referred to the General Purposes Committee, Eventually it was decided to refer the matter back and the minutes, with this exception, were passed STREET MAKING OISPUTE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, a letter was read froui Mr. J. C. Ridgway in reference to the account due from him for street making, in which Mr. Ridgway stated that he understood the £6O agreed to be accepted by this Comfhittee was in settlement of the total amount 'due from him for paving not only the. passage behind Hepherd-street. but the passage behind LiverpOol-road, and the Town Clerk was instructed to I inform Mr. Ridgway that the Committee clearly under. stood that the £6O which they had agreed to accept without prejudice, was in respect of the p issage behind Hepherd-street only, and that unless the amount due from him is paid within seven days, proceedings will be taken for the recovery of the whole amount due from him, without any reduction. At a subsequent meeting Colonel Ridgway and his solicitor (Mr. Forshaw) again waited upon the committee in reference to the expenses incurred in the paving of the passage behind Liverpool- road, and stated that they were both under the iMpres- sion that the £6O which was agreed to at the last meeting at which they attended was in full settlement of the Corporation's claim in respect of the passages behind Elepherd-street and Liverpool-road. After fully considering the matter the committee decided to accept the sum of £25 in settlement of the expenses due in respect of the paving of the passage behind Liverpool- road, this sum representing a reduction in the same pro- portion as the d'mount allowed on the expenses for the paving of the passage behind Nepherd-street. Alderman BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes. Councillor CLEGG moved that the recommendation be referred back. To interfere with the final opportion- ments made by the Paving and Sewerage Committee and confirmed by the Council would lead to serious trouble by way of appeals. If the Council granted the reduction and approved the principle they would have owners constantly disputing their accounts and members of the committee would be subjeuted to influences that tended to demoralize publicilife. I At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, Joseph Abrahams, forge labourer, 10. Dial-court, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-court on the iprevious evening, and with assulting P.C. Gilchrist.— Gilchrist stated that he was on duty in Dial-court when he saw the prisoner, who was drunk and acting in a very disorderly manher. He asked him to go away, and he refused, and said he would "stop where he was." Prisoner subsequently struck him on the head and knocked his (the officer's) hat off. H closed wita him on the giound. P.C. Hughes cause to his assistance. Prisoner was in the habit of pulling people by the arm and asking them for money.—Prisoner : "It is a lie ; that is all I have to say : it is no use talking ;I never struck the oilicer." Prisoner went on to say that he had been roughly handled by the police, and that his wrist had been injured.—Dr. Fox I (to the prisoner) : I saw you last night at 5.30, and must confess that I thought the officers used you a little bit roughly in the use of the handcuffs. It appeared to me there was undue severity. Persons coming along the street at the time accosted rue and made the same I remark. Do you complain of your wrist ?—Prisoner said that he did not that morning. Ha was willing to "let that go."—The Chairman : The serious part of this is that you have assaulted the police. We must support the authorities. You will be fined 10s., and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. WARRINGTON INCORRIG DM ES. —FATH ER'S CH A RITABLE WISH. •

At the Borough Police Court on i'n-esday two notori- ous characters—Patrick Richard Moran and Elias Hurst —were charged with frectibenting Dallam-lane early that morning for an unlawful purpose, viz., to commit a felony--Superintendent Monaghan stated that Mr. W. J. Shaw, the licensee of the Greyhound Inn, a beer- house at the corner of Buckley-street, made his premises secure at 11.25 on Monday night, and retired to rest. At 12.15 hearing a noise, he got up, dressed, and leoked round, but as everything appeared to he right,he retired to rest. Shortly afterwards he %VP; knocked up by John Flynn and Edward Brochick. Flynn said he was returning home from his work, when he saw the prisoners and another man standing near Mr. Shaw's window. Flynn spoke to them. and went home, but as soon as begot into the house. he heard a sound similar to that of breaking glass. Ho at once went out and saw the prisoners and another man running away. He knocked Mr. Shaw up, and it was found that his kitchen window had been broken near the catch, but the prisoners were unable to get into the house, as the catch was a patent one. Mr. Shaw got up, and he and Flynn and Brodrick went in search of the prisoners, and found them near the Three Pigeons. The police I were sent for, and Sergeant Evans came on the scene and arrested the prisoners.- -Mr. Shaw corroborated this statement, and said that Moran's father had been to see him that morning, and said he trusted that their Worships would give his son 20 years imprisonment,if possible. (Laughter)—Further evidence having been given Moran denied having been near the Greyhound Inn and said he was going home when arrested.—Hurst : I wont let this lad have all the blame; Idid it all.—(Laughter).—Moran : You did not do it.—(Renewed laughter).—Superintendent Monaghan said that Moran had an awful career and had been 30 times before the Court for different offences. He was most incorrigible and was in fact, the worst , character in the town. Hurst commenced his career in Widnes some years ago,and be did nothing but prowl about the country, committing thefts and begging. He asked the bench in the interests of the public, to send 1 these men away, RS they were prowling the streets all night through.—The Bench committed prisoners to gaol for a month each, with hard labour, and thanked the , witnesses for their services to the police.

Alderman BENNETT : Very yell, I will talk for the sake of talking, as you often do. (Laughter.) Con- tinuing he said the reduction would make it easier for local manufacturers to extend their enterprise. A works was recently built in Warrington and the firm installed their own electricity and the Corporation were deprived of a large customer simply because they could not supply cheaply enough. The use of electricity would also mitigate the smoke nuisance. Councillor LORD withdrew the motion and the minutes were approved, Alderman SME THURST remark- irug that if the Corporation had to depend on the light- ing customers they might as well close the works. THE DEPUTY TOWN CLERK.

HONORARIUM AND INCREASE OF SALARY. Thefollowing resolution of the General Purposes Committee was presented :—" That the salary hf the Deputy Town Clerk be increased as and nom the 25th ult. to £2OO, and that he be granted an honorarium of £5O for the efficient manner in which he carried out the work of the department during the absence of the Town Clerk." The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes. Councillor CFIANI'LER said be understood when the Town Clerk was granted leave of absence they would never have such an application as that to consider. He thought that while the Town Clerk was away the work was done by the other officials.

The Meioit You don't expect them to work for nothing. Councillor CRANTLER : They are getting well paid at present. I call this a gratuity and I don't believe in any officials of the Corporation receiving gratuities. When you consider the salaries some are getting, we are really psving them more for the positions 1 than Cabinet Ministers receive, in proportion to the ' work they do and the population they have control of. Continuing Councillor Chantler said he believed the Deputy Town Clerk was one of their best officials but there was such a thing as treating people too well. Some members of the Council might be inclined to vote for it, but if it came to their own private affairs would they be so willing to grant it ? How many hours had the extra vrerk inconvenienced Mr. Hallaway? The MAYOR : Look at the extra committees. Councillor CELorrfaca : And look at the honour attached to it. He is fit to be a Town Clerk anywhere hnw, Councillor Chantler moved that the minute be referred back as even if he were inclined to grant an honorarium it would not be as much as £5O. There was no seconder of theamepdment which there- fore fell to the ground. Councillor &row said it had been suggested by rate- payers—but he did not associate himself with it—that the honorarium should be paid by the Town Clerk because the extra duties were entailed by his having leave of absence. He (Councillor Stott) supported the motion because he felt Mr. Hallaway had done extra work and he believed in men being paid for extra work, whether they were officials or ordinary employees. Mr. Hallaway was well deserving of some extra recompense for his work in regard to the Distress Co:nmittee, the prosecution of a Councillor, and other important matters which had occupied him until late in the even- ing. He (Councillor Stott) would, however, like to mentionfthat last week he went down Orford-avenue to watch the Corporation work in progress there. He saw men twenty feet below the surface who after they had been working half an hour were wet through almost to the waist. He wondered whether the Council would have been so generous to those men—the best paid of whom received 21s. a week—if they had required leavb of absence for three months. While agreeing to the grant to the Deputy Town Clark he would insist on I consideration being shown to low-paid employees. The MAYOR said that when these workmen worked extra hours they were paid extra. The Deputy Toyer' Clerk worked extra time and therefore he should be I paid for it. In a sudden emergency Mr. Hallaway was I called upon to act in a superior position and he per-) formed the duties so well that he had satisfied everyone' According to the scale his salary was £l9O but the com- mittee found that he was such a good servant that he I was worth considerably more than they bargained with him for and therefore recommended the advance to £2OO. He would still be receiving £lOO a year less than wasipaid to Mr. Stanley Wilson. He had a great deal of overtime to put in and, much anxiety in connection with investigation committees and concerning the recent prosecution. He (the Mayor) did not think £5O was too much to cover practically his out of pocket expenses. The TOWN CLERK said he thought Mr. Hallaway was well entitled to the payment of an honorarium. If it was the wish of the Council he (Mr. Whittle) would pay it out of his own pocket (Cries of" No "). Councillor STOTT : Ido not oppose the grant in any way. I appreciate the work done and lam willing that the honorarium should be granted. Other employees should however, have the same eonsideration. Councillor LORD : Other employees of the Corpora- tion have been treated on similar lines, and I for one shall insist that they are so treated. Ido not believe 'in drawing a line between officials and workmen. The MAYOR: They ought all to be paid according to the value of the work they do. The committee's recommendation was then approved. WORKMEN'S TRAM FARES. ••• HALFPENNY TICKETS SANCTIONED. Baby Treated at Two Hospitals Over a Year Eyes Grew Worse—Doctor Said They Might Be Bad for Years.

div.head: ONE BOX OF CUTICURA MAKES COMPLETE CURE
div.p: ONE BOX OF CUTICURA MAKES COMPLETE CURE

"When my little girl was a few months old, her eyes began to get bad; thinking it was from her teeth, I lived in hopes of them getting better, but as they did not improve I decided to get medical advice. I took her to the Hospital several times, and subsequently to the Children's Hospital at —, to which institution I took her for twelve months. The doctors were most,kind and attentive, and did all they could for her, but her eyes seemed to be growing worse. One doctor told me they might be bad for years; I was very miserable at such a prospect. I was one day stopped in the street by a Mrs. Todd who told me that Cuticura Oint- ment had cured her boy, and advised me to try it. I commenced using it that very night. The cure has been marvellous. The eyes soon commenced to get strong, and they are now as healthy as if there had never been anything the matter with them. The cure was completed with less than one box of Cuticura Ointment. You are at liberty to make what use you like of this letter, and I trust it may be the means of others being cured as my little girl has been.— Mrs. F. Phillips, Grafton St., Waverly, Sydney, N. S. W." Refer- ence, Messrs. R. Towns S.: Co., Sydney.

Anglicanism, there would be no Roman I Catholicism, there would be no Methodism with- out dogmatism. It seems like stating a truism, but it has never been said bAfore from the Front Bench Of either side of the House. Mr.,BraaELL, simply took the bit:in .his teeth. He said in plain direct, incontrovertible words what everybody who has thought on the subject knows to be true. His point is that we caimot exclude dogma from the schools, but that we can and must exclude denomi- nationalism,denominationalism being the difference expressed long ago between " your doxy ' "and my dozy.' " Mr. BIRRELL is most strongly in favcrir of religious teaching in the schools,but he wants this teaching to unite) on those things on which all Christians are agreed. This, surely, is possible,and if it is possible the religious difficulty in education is at an end.

Liberals cannot look with THE ALDERMANIC any satisfaction on the ELEcnoN. result of the Aldermanic election at Tuesday's Council meeting, and taking all the circumstances into consideration there will be some degree of bitterness in the mike of the party. The vacancy was filled by the elevation of Councillor W. J. Forshaw, who was less entitled to the honour than at least three Liberals, i.e. Councillors Ellison, Duncan, and Burton. Councillor Ellison was the Liberal candidate at the last election—in February —when he was defeated solely by reason of the Non-Trading vote being cast solidly against him. The same thing happened again on Tuesday. We have no desire to rake up the causes which have made Councillor Ellison unacceptable to the Non-Traders—though we deplore them exceedingly for they have deprived a worthy Councillor of the honour to which nine years of useful public service entitle him. But the fact remains that Councillor Ellison had no chance of being elected, and this was so well known by the Liberal leaders that we believe, until almost the last minute, they had intended to run Councillor Duncan, whose claim to the seat was practically on all fours with that of the defeated candidate. We feel bound to condemn the unwisdorn of the stubborn policy which resulted in the seat being lost to the party. Coun- cillor i 'Duncan was assured the Non-Ttaders', as well as the Liberal support, and we think it was the duty of our party managers to make sure of the seat. To all intents and purposes, the aldermanie elections are now conducted on party lines, with the important difference from old experience that there are three parties in the field to-day instead of two. It is no use " kicking against the pricks," and we regret that the wisdom which is looked for in party management, was, on this occasion, conspicuous by its absence to the detriment of the status of Liberalism in the town.

There is some danger of VOTES FOR WOMEN. OUT correspondent, Mr. , Osborne, mistaking the shadow for the substance. Our criticism of the "savage suffragettes" and the conduct which has brought them into the hands of the police was, we still think, necessarily severe. But in con- demning some of the methods of these ladies we would not have it thought for a moment that we I were showing hostility to the movement which they have at heart. "Votes for women " is a cry with which we have full sympathy. Women with the responsibilities of citizenship are entitled to claim a vote, and we hope that the present Government will find time, ere it relinquishes office' to bring in a Bill which will extend the franchise to these members of the fair sex. What we deprecate is the unseemly conduct of those advocates of the cause who persist in annoying Mr. Asquith, who create a disturbance in the streets, and who refuse to give any guarantee to keep the peace. Appar- ently a few weeks' martyrdom in gaol is a sine qua non to the object they have in view. If it is endured to arouse public sympathy, we think the sacrifice is in vain. These ladies can make very effective protests against what they deem official apathy without wilfully disturbing the peace and going to gaol in imaginary triumph. We hope they will eventually see the force of this and not persist in using such extreme measures as, in our opinion, set back, rather than advance, the cause of Woman's Suffrage.
Should the Corporation THE INFIRMARY. contribute towards _ the

maintenance of the Infir- mary? This is a question which was raised in the Town Council by Councillor Wright,and at first thought most people will be inclined to answer in the affirmative. The question is, however, not quite so simple as it seems. Such an institution as the borough infirmary ought to be maintained out of the rates and controlled by the munici- pality. But there is no suggestion to take over the Infirmary " lock, stock, and barrel." The fact that it is maintained by voluntary subscriptions is not one to be regretted, so long as the subscriptions are adequate, but for, years the institution has suffered tor want of money. Tha big extension scheme now on hand—though it is being nobly subscribed to—aggravates the posi- tion and provides matter for earnest consideration on the part of all those interested in the welfare of the institution. Councillm Wright's proposal is that the Corporation shall make a grant of £l,OOO or £2,000 to the Infirmary from the public funds. This it cannot do without going to Parliament for special authority. However, the Liverpool Cor- poration has managed to find a way of Icontributing to a similar object, and we are glad that the matter is to be further considered by the General Purposes Committee of the Warrington Town Council. An aspect of the case which does not immediately occur to everyone is this. If the Corporation contributes to the extension scheme then those ratepayers who have already bulked largely in the subscription list will be paying twice. We do not consider this an insuperable objection but there is a good 'deal in the conten- tion that the Infirmary should be either on the rates entirely, or depend wholly on voluntary effort. These are points which we hope the Com- mittee will weigh carefully in considering the not unreasonable application for a grant from the public fuuds. The Warrington . Training

THE POSITION OF College authorities are THE TEACHER. fortunate in invariably securing the services of well- known educationists for their aimual'priz9-giving. On Saturday they were honoured with .a visit from Sir Henry Hibbert who by reason of his important office of chairman of the Lancashire County. Educa- tion Committee is particularly well qualifiel. to speak on matters of :moment in the educational world. It is no light task to control the delibera- tions of an authority representing the marked diversities of opinion which must necessarily manifest themselves in such a large area, but it is Sir Henry's pardonable boast that friction has been practicable unknown on the committee' As befitted the occasion, his address on Saturday was devoted mainly to a consideration of the posi- tion of the teacher which has undeniably improved of late years. In the Lancashire County Educa- tion area the teachers are being paid in salaries £50,000. more that they were receiving in 190:2 and in addition the staffs have been increaqed to the extent of £40,000. No one grudges the members of this worthy profession adequate rennmeration for work which becomes increasingly important as time goes on. It is noOrious that a great many teachers have been ill-paid in the past and, as an act of justice, they required to be placed on a better footing. At present the prospects of the 1 profession are of the brightest and a factor which I should not be overlooked is that the extension of I the Secondary system is opening the way to more lucrative, spheres of labour to those who have the ambition and talents to qualify themselves. From the ratepayer's point of view, the question which- concerns him most is whether he is getting value I for money. If he sees our educational system making rapid strides he will not be disposed to complain, but it behoves Education Authorities to administer their funds carefully and wisely with

ST. HELENS ENGINEERS. FAREWELL TO COLONEL MURRAY.

There were many striking evidences of esteem and affection for Colonel J. D. Murray shown by the mem- bers of the 2nd Lancashire Royal Engineers (Volun- teers) on Sunday, when the commanding officer took leave of the regiment after sixteen years with the corps, the last six as commander—at the conclusion of the annual church parade at St. Thomas's Church. The service was conducted by Acting-Chaplain the Rev. L. J. Rich, and the sermon preached by the Rev. J. P. Baines, M A., V.D.. Acting-Chaplain to the Mersey Division of the R.E.V. About 300 men were present on parade.—The Rev. J. P. Baynes, preaching on " Ancient Battlecries," said he felt it a privilege to be with them that morning at what must be to many of them a memorable church parade, and to give them the spmpathy of a comrade in the parting which they knew was to take place that day.—When the regiment returned to headquarters they were drawn up in quarter- column on the drill ground.—Colonel Murray urged them to go on striving to make it the best corps in the kingdom. He wished them God-speed.—Major Sayce said he was sure the regiment would wish him to express the extreme regret with which they heard of Colonel Murrao's retirement. They were all very sorry, but it must be satisfactory to the colonel to know that he could hand to his successor a thoroughly up-to-date corps, efficient and equipped in the best way. —The regiment afterwards lined the route to the officers' mess' and as Colonel Murray proceeded to the mess the band of the regiment played "Acid Lang Syne." The col- lection in church for the Parish Nurses' Fund realised over £ L

'PRESENTATION TO THE REV. F. W. CLARKE. The Rev. F. W. Clarke, 8.A., ,Aho has been pastor of the St. Helens Congregational Church for seven years, in succession to the late Rev. J. A. Mitchell, preached his farewell sermons yesterday, when there were large congregations. In the afternoon Mr. Clarke was pre- sented by the officers and teachers of the Sunday school with a handsome study chair. At the morning service Mr. Clarke preached from two texts, " Our fellowship" and" Walk worthily of God," and said that the fellow- ship that had existed between the minister and his church was one of the greatest rewards of the ministry, and was something to thank God for in connection with his pastorate there. Looking back over his ministry, he felt that they had been on the whole happy and fruitful years, and he was . glad that he came them They had worked together and worshipped together, and fought I side by side together, and had sorrowed and rejoiced together. He thanked God for the measure of success whichhad attended his ministry amongst them, and for the great liberality which had been displayed. During last week the weekly offerings reached, he believed, the highest point on record. it might be asked why, then, was he going. He had to confess he found it hard at times to answer that question especially considering the many expressions of regret on his leaving which had been tendered to him. Yet he had now no doubt that the decision to adhere to his resignation was the right one. It might be that the reasons in one's own mind were not the only reasons which existed for the step. A higher wisdom than they possessed might be directing them. STEALING BOOTS AT ST. HELENS. ALLEGED GANG OF THIEVES.

Frederick Smith and Thomas Honey were charged on two informations at St.Helens on Tuesday with stealing boots from outside shops on Saturday night, and Frank Riley, of Bolton-street, was charged with receiving the articles.—The Chief Constable said that the , evidence pointed to a systematic series of thefts, On Saturday night two men who were in Church-street saw Smith take the boots, while Honey stood in front of Smith and covered his movements. The men were watched,and they took boots from Messrs. Baker's shop inChurch-street and from Haylock's shop in Bridge-street. Then Police • constable Bate was informed and he arrested Smith.— A somewhat painful scene took placs when Michael Honey, aged ten, was called to give evidence.—Honey land Riley , said it was a shame to call the lad.—The magistrates asked if it was absolutely necessary.—The Chief Constable said it was. He appreciated the diffi- cult position the lad was in, but it was high time that this gang was smashed up. Smith and Riley were related to Honey Ly marriage. They were robbing !right Itnd left, and it ought to be stopped.—The lad at I first contradicted the statement he had made to the police but afterwards he said that the statement that he tools the boots to Riley's house was true.: Detective Roe said that when he confronted Riley with the boy the lad told him that he gave him the boots.— Riley protested that this was quite wrong, and that there were witnesses who would contradict the lad's statements. He insisted that he should be sent to the assizes for trial.—The Chief Constable mentioned that Riley was one of the three men who were sentenced to death in 1894 for the murder of P.C. Gordon.—The magistrates fined Smith £2 or twenty-eight days. and sent Honey to gaol for four months' hard labour. Riley was discharged, the chairman telling him that he had had a near squeak, and they would caution him once more. They thought he was guilty, but the evidence was not quite suflicient.

ST. HELENS WOMAN'S DEATH. ALLEGED NEGLECT BY A MIDWIFE. EVIDENCE AT THE INQUEST. By the coroner's orders, a jury of fifteen was empanelled at the Town Hall, St. Helens, on Monday, when the inquiry was opened into the death of Mrs. Ruth Dinah Gibson, of 07, Hoole Bank-street, Parr.— Mr. Brighouse said it would be necessary for the inquest to be opened, and then to be adjourned, and he proposed, unless there was some very stroaig objection on the part of the jury, that the inquiry should be adjourned until 1 Friday afternoon.lt was absolutely necessary that there 1 should be on adjournment in order to get 111 the informa- tion that theylcould. Ruth Dinah Gibson was a married 1 woman, and she died at half-past eleven on Saturday night last at the Providence Hospital. It seemed that on June 9th last she gave birth to twins, and in conse- quence of a statement she made to Dr. O'Keefe, and in consequence of the evidence that the police had already obtained, it became a question whether the midwife who attended her in her confinement, was not criminally responsible for her death. It was alleged that she was in a state of intoxication at the time, and that she did things that she ought not to have done. It was a case that would require some very careful inquiries at the bands of the jury. He proposed to lhave a post-mortem examination made by two medical men, and in the meantime the police %could collect all the evidence, which would be put before them, and then they could decide what course to adopt in the case.- -The Foreman : Is this woman a certificated mid- wife ?—The Coroner : I don't know.—Detective Stave- ley : Yes, she is, sir.—The Coroner said the jury would understand that he was not stating any of the alleged facts at present, because that would be mani- festly unfair to the midwife. The proper coarse was to have the N% itnesses brought before them and put in the box, and let them on their oath tell their own story in their own way. He did not want any statements that were not true to get out to the public.—The jury were then bound over to appear on Friday.

LIKED DRINK BETTER THAN WORK. At Warrington on Wednesday, John Ayres was sent to gaol for one month for absconding from the borough and leaving his child chargeable to the union. It was stated that the child's maintenance, and also that of another,during their stay in the workhouse had cost the town over £lOO, to which sums prisoner had not con- tributed a penny. He was deshribed by Superintendent ,Monahan as a man who liked drink batter than work.

" The inhabitants of this court ought to have gold medals. , Ananias and Sapphira would be perfect bungling apprentices I.4eside them," was the remark of the Chester Coroner at an inquiry this week into the death of a rag-gatherer's wife. * * * The taste for the beautiful has evidently reached as far as Fearnhcad for in the re-making of the roads leading to Cinnamon Brow the opportunity has been taken to make a mound in the centre of the road on which shrubs are being planted by some of the residents. * * * The removal of the War Office Department from Pall Mall to Whitehall will begin shortly. The sug- gestion that the authorities should sell the furniture in use at the old building and repurchase it at an enhanced price for the new one has been declinetl.— " Punch.' -

* * * There should be a fine opportunity for the Labour Party to capture " the Seat" on Saturday next, when all the Liberals and Conservatives will be at South- port and Blackpool. That is, of course, if the mem- bers of the Labour Party have not also managed to get cheap tickets for the seaside ! * * One Town Councillor in alluding to Alderman Smethurst's sensational statement that there was last year a loss of.C.,l6per week on the Sankey Bridges tram route, said it was a heavy " defishit." Most people will agree with his meaning. Halfpenny. fares or halfpenny stiges, or some other experiment, are needed.

* ** "I am for the State providing secular education alone, and leaving it to parents and pastors to teach religion to children. lam convinced that we shall eventually have to come to this, if the schoolhouse is not to be for ever the battle ground of rival sects to the great injury to the cause of religion."—Mr. Labouchere in " Truth." * * We are getting quite used to the launching of vessels in the neighbourhood. It is only a little over a year since the good ship " Eustace Carey " left the stocks at Sankey Bridges and on Thursday the" Santa Rosa "was launched amid scenes of great enthusiasm. Such events serve to recall the old days when ship- building was one of Warrington's great industries. *s* Councillor Lord had the laugh against him on Tuesday. The Chairman of the Sanitary Committee had just been mentioning a tender which had been accepted for scrap iron when Councillor Lord jumped up and said " Is this the lowest tender ?" The Chair- man replied : "No, it is the highest !" and Coun- cillor Lord had to join in the laugh against himself. * * * The Paving and Sewerage Committee are going to make another experiment with tarred macadam, but not in Sankey-street. This time Museum-street has been chosen, and as the street is a quiet one, we pre- sume it will be closed for a time to give the new macadam a chance to set. There is still a quantity of the other rubbish in Sankey-street crying aloud to the heavens and to the committee for removal.

MOTHERS AT SOUTHPORT. Lqst Thursday the Mother's Meeting connected with St. John's Church held their annual picnic, Southport being selected for the rendezvous. Favoured by beauti- ful weather the attractions of Southport proved irresistible and the mothers bade very enjoyable outing, MORE STREET BETTING.

Frank Dale, an old offender, who did not appear, was summoned at Newton Petty Sessions for street betting at Earlestown, on June llth.—P.S. Barrow deposed that he was on duty in Sankey-street, and sav Dale, in Back Earle-street, take slips and money from thrf 3 different men between 2.15 and 2.20. When he saw witness he ran away and would not stop though witness shouted to him.—Fined .£5 and costs. THE BOY, THE AIR GUN, AND THE LAMP.

* * * Alderman Smethurst hardly gets fair play, even from the Mayo. But it if difficult to take him seriously always. On Tuesday he was very much nettled at a Tramways Committee meeting being styled a hole and corner affair. He rose to his feet and said angrily, and contemptuously, that he should treat the remark with perfect silence. The joke is how- ever, that the Alderman immediately launched into an excited protest against the insult, which took some minutes to deliver. * * * - - -

The Deputy Town Clerk has done well out of his temporary toten-clerkship. An honorarium of £5O was granted him on Tuesday "for the efficient manner in which he carried out the work of the department during the absence of the Town Clerk." In addition his salary has been raised to £2OO, though only so recently as April 25th it was raised from .V. 75 to £l9O. We are glad to see that the Council ,realises that it has a smart servant in Mr. Hallaway, and also that he was by no means over-paid, for a professional man.

* ,k Next Saturday there will be a great exodus from Warrington as a result of the two great picnics organised by the Liberal and Conservative forces in the town. Our contemporary, the "Observer," endeavoured to he sarcastic in its last issue at the cheapness of the Liberal trip to Sonthport. It said : " The poverty of the Conservative party in Warring- ton seems amply demonstrated from the fact that they are charging ss. 61 for the Blackpool trip, while the abundant wealth in which the Liberal party wallow is evidenced by the fact that some 2,000 members of the Liberal Association, the Women's Liberal Association, Junior Liberal Association, and the Progressive Labour League are to have their outing to Southport at the nominal charge of Is. per head. It is significantly announced that the " Member for the Borough will, of course, be present."—Now, we could have understood a natural feeling of envy causing such an allusion to I the rival treat. But a motive is imputed, of which I the Tories are of course quite guiltless. A 55.16 d. ticket does seem rather dear compared with one at is, I but when the former can he had for nothing, the com- parison is on a different footing. We are credibly Informed that some of these ss. Gd. Tory tickets have been obtained without any equivalent in hard cash. Probably, the ex-member of the borough will be present—to paraphrase our contemporary's final comment.

Police and Post Office. Teams representing the above met at cricket on th 3,. Police ground On Thursday. The police declared at 58 for 8, and the Post Office men totalled 46, all out. Success of an Old Warringtonian. Mr. W. Langshaiv, formerly a scholar and pupil teacher at the Warrington National SAlbol, and after- wards assistant at the Warrington People's -College- has since had a ',very successful career as headmaster of the Wigan National and Blue Coat School. By his, latest successes his scholars have now won no less• than one hundred Grammar School Free Scholarships entitling the holders to free education for three years; also for eight years in succession the " Holt " Scholar- ship tenable for four years has been won by his boys. These scholarships represent a total monetary value of something like £3,000 a record of which any school- master might well feel proud. Many of these boys have since gained Universit) and other distinctions. During the twentv-4ight years Mr. Latigsliaw has had charge of the sclool the highest results have invari- ably been _ maintained, and ,some years ago when • schools were excused the annual examination' for a successi.m of excellent results Mr. Langshaw's was the first school in Wigan to receive that"honotir for - which he received the commendation of the late Wigan School Board.

society of Chemical Industry to Visit War- rington. Next Thursday vill be a notable day in the history of Messrs Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited. The Society of Chemical Industry is holding its annual meetings in Manchester during the week and Thursday has been decided upon for a visit to Messrs. Crosfield's works. The delegates, who will number about 350; will arrive at the works at 11.5 a.m„ and will be con- ducted through the various departments. The many interesting processes will be explained and all the visitors will be furnished with printed guide books. At 1.30 luncheon will be served in the workmen's dining hall and at 2.30 there will be a Fire Brigade and Ambulance demonstration and an exhibition of• physical drill by a squad of the Works Volunteer Company. During the afternoon parties will be made up of persons interested in special subjects and they will have the,opportnnity of inspecting these branches of the Company's work. The Works Band will play seleations in the yard. and in the recreation room there 4 will be a concert by the orchestra,and mixed and male voice choirs, and a gymnastic display by girls. At 3.30 tea will be served in the roof garden and in the girls' dining room and the visitors will depart at 4.15. Warrington P.S.A - Mr. C. Drink water presided at the weekly meeting of the WarringtonP.S.AlSociety which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street on Sunday and spoke of the good he had personally received at the meetings of the P.S.A. Mr. E. Wynne Jones delivered an address on " Brotherhood," and stated that what was needed to-day was a revival of the old social conscience - as it was set forth in the Gospel, and cause it to permeate the life of the'nation. They must reaffirm with no uncertain voice the great principle of Christian brotherhood. As they looked around them how little real feeling of equality did they find ! What foolish airs some people gave themselves., as if God had not made of one blood' all men. They must get back to the principles• of Jesus Christ, and, although churches had been charged with being so much concerned about the "life to come "that they had no time to think of making the present life any better, in face of that he believed the churches were getting back to the principles of Christ, and were taking a greater interest in all that concerned the life of the people. I hey were entering on a new era, an era of effort after' a better organiza- tion of the community, which should secure more general wellbeing for all, and a wider diffusion of all that made for the welfare of humanity.--Mr. Willett rendered two solos in a very efficient manner. Mr. B. Wadsworth was the accompanist. Mr.W.Light and Councillor Clegg also took part in the service.
