div.head: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY.
Messrs Armitage and Rigby.

On Saturday a large number of the emnlnyees of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby (Cockhedg,e Mills) and friends had an enjoyable trip to Southport. The majority of the party plumed back the same evening, but others remair.ed for the week-end.

div.head: Wesleyan Teachers at Delamere. . . .
div.p: Wesleyan Teachers at Delamere. . . .

The Sunday wschool teachers of the Bold-street and Penketh WesleyariSchools had a very successful outing to Delamere on Saturday. The party numbered over 70 and Wa9 accompanied by the Revs. J. Manning and A. C. Parker. The drive through the beautiful Cheshire country was thoroughly enjoyed. Tea was provided at the picturesquely situated Eddi4bury Lodge and alto- gether the outing was a complete success and will be long remembered with pleasure by all who took part:

Buckley Street P.S.A. Society. The members of the Buckley-street P.S.A. Society had a picnic to Llangollen on Saturday. The party to the number of about 30, left Bank Quay Station at 7.15 in a saloon carriage accompanied by Mr. Andrew Jennings (superintendent), and Mr. it. Leech (secre- tary), Llangollen being reached in good time. The visitors drove to the Horse Shoe Falls and returned for dinner to the ivon Hotel, and later in the day ascended Crow Hill, and also visited the Abbey. Tea was partaken of at the hotel. A start for home was made at 7.15, and Warrington was safely reached at half- past nine. The weather throughout the day was line, and the members of the society voted the outing a com- plete success. Monks, Hall and Co.

Southport was the destination of the employ6S of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., to the number of about eleven hundred. A start was made shortly after seven o'clock from Bank Quay Railway Station, and the party arrived at Southport at about nine o'clock. Excellent weather prevailed throughout the day, and the workmen and their wives and families thoroughly enjoyed themselves. A good number paid a visit to the beautiful Cemetery, and to Kerr Gardens. The water chute attracted a great amount of interestand patronage along with the various classes of amusement provided for the general public on the Southport sands. A delightful day was too soon brought to a close, and the return journey to Warrington was commenced shortly after half•past nine, Warrington being safely reached at 11.15.

div.head: St. Ann's Church Choir.
div.p: St. Ann's Church Choir.

Success attended the annual trip in crinnection with this choir Which took place on Saturday. The party, numbering 46, left the Central Station at 7 a.m.. bound for Matlock Bath, which was reached shortly before 10 o'clock. The weather, which had been dull and unsettled, turned out beautifully fine and warm, and during the dav visits were paid to the numerous places of interest for which Matlock is noted, chiefly. the Heights of Abraham, Lovers' Walk, gardens and cliffs, High Tor, and the lead mines existing in the interior of the mountains. As on the two previous visits, the catering was again in The hands of Messrs. P. Dalton and Son, of the Central Hotel. The return journey, which commenced shortly after 7 p.m., included a pleasant hour at Chinley, and home was reached at 9.30 n.rn., after a most enjoyable day. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. E. A. Padmore. organist and choirmaster of St. Ann's Church.

div.head: William Robertson Limited, Latchford.
div.p: William Robertson Limited, Latchford.

The fourth annual picnic in connection with this company took place on Saturday last to Blackpool, this being the third visit to that place. The party,nuraber- in,g about 130, went by snecial cars from Latchford Swing Bridge, and left Bank Quay Station about 7 o'clock, arriving at Blackpool after a good ride at 9 o'clock. The weather was fine, being a most pleasurable contrast to that experienced on the day of the last picnic, when rain prevailed during the greater part of the day. During the morning the parry divided to various enjoyments, all leading to a good appetite for the dinner which had been arranged for at the Winter Gardens. This was served at 11.30 a.m. and the party seemed in good form to enjoy it. A pleasing circum- stance in connection with the function was that the party were favoured with the presence of Mr. Robertson, the chairman and managing director of the company, and Mrs. Robertson. Mr. Wareing, the manager, and Mrs. Wareing were also present, and Mr. Collins, the secretary.and IMrs.Collins.The dinner was very tastefully and invitingly served and was enjoxed most thoroughly. —After the repast Mr. Robertson delivered a few words to the company. He thanked them for their invitation and said it gave him very great pleasure to be amongst them, and he hoped they would make the most of the day, and return home with a full sense of enjoyment.— Mr. Collins on behalf of the men said he did not think it gave Mr. and Mrs. Robertson any greater pleasure to come than it did to the party to be favoured with their presence. He also thanked Mr. and Mrs. Wareing for attending.and remarked that the presence of Mr. Rober- tson aid Mr. Wareing proved their deep interest in the welfare of the employees, and that they took a pleasure in participating in their enjoyrnent.—Mr.Robertson and Mr. Wareing in turn responded to these remarks, and they both expressed great pleasure at the good arrange- ments which bad been made by the managers of the I picnic, Mr. Collins and Mr. Humphreys. One of the company also expressed the best thanks of all the party for the excellent dinner and the splendid manner in which it was served.—The arty then dispersed to go their different ways to We the various sights and attractions of the town, which were well enjoyed. The return journey was cornmencedsat 8.50 p.m., and War- rington was reached at 11 p.m., all going home with pleasant memories of a very happy day.

Wall Collapses—Workmen Injured.

A remark-able accident occurred at eight o'clock on Monday evening. P.O. Leonard was on duty in Springfield-street when he heard the noise as of some- thing falling in the direction of the new post office in course of erection there. Cries for "help "immediately followed. The officer went with all speed to the post office and found that the brick wall separating Mr. Charlie White's garden from the new building had collapsed and almost buried three workmen who had been at work near it. With assistance the men were extricated and by order of Dr. Joseph, who was quickly on the scene, two of them were conveyed in the horse ambulance to the Infirmary in charge of Sergeant Williamson and two constables. The names of the injured men are Richard Moor, who sustained a fractured collar bone, and Edward Austin whose back and tide were contused. Richard Hall escaped with a shaking. All the men hail from Blackpool, being employed by Messrs. Parkinson Ltd.,contractors, of that town. It appears that they were engaged in making a concrete foundation near the wall when the accident happened. , LAWN TEENER, CROQUET, and other outdoor sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge-st.—Advt. Appleton Rifle Club. _ _ - -

_ On Saturday the monthly competition was held at the Range, when the following contests took place : Medal Competition : 10 shots at a stationery target, 3-inch Bull, ond 10 shots at a disappearing target ; distance 100 yards ; fired with the service rifle :- Ist prize, Mr. J. Wilcox; 2nd, Mr. A. Down. Open Sweep-Stakes : 5 shots at 100 yards, 3-inch bull :- Ist prize, Mr. J. W. Plinston ; 2nd, Mr. A. Down. Members' Stakes: 7 shots, in addition ta a sighting shot, at 100 yards, 6-inch bull : —lst prize, Mr. J. W. Plinston ; 2nd, Mr. J. Wilcox. An interesting com- petition is in progress every Saturday except the, last Saturday in each month, for the "Rifleman " Certifi- cates, issued by the National Rifle Association. To gain one of these certificates it is necessary to make a score of 114 points, out of a possible 150. Thirty shots must be fired, 10 at each of these distances, or 20 at one distance and 10 at another, or 30 may be fired at one distance. In the case of a miniature ' range, as at Appleton, miniatnre rifles or service rifles, with Morris tubes or adaptors must be used. Up to the present, no member. of the Appleton Club has made the necessary score, the highest haying been 112 paints, but better results are anticipated. div.head: SEQUEL TO A COLLISION.
div.p: SEQUEL TO A COLLISION.

THOUGHT, SIGHT, HEARING, TOUCH. Dr. Symes Thompson says the length of time taken in communicating by touch is one-seventh of a second before there is a consciousness of the touch. When a sound is heard the interval is one-sixth of a second; when an object is seen the interval is one-fifth of a second; in the case of a thought it is one-fortieth of a second.

div.head: MOUNTAIN SICKNESS.
div.p: MOUNTAIN SICKNESS.

According to the results of recent expert obi servations at high altitudes, the diminished ten- sion of the oxygen of the atmosphere clogs the process of oxidation, and this sets up an elabora- tion of poisonous substances, the retention of which causes symptoms of self-poisoning, and accounts for the symptoms of mountain sickness. Acclimatisation, however, results in a few days, ' and the symptoms pass away under circum- stances resembling these accompanying the pass. ing of the crisis in infectious maladies.

div.head: OBEDIENCE OF BEES.
div.p: OBEDIENCE OF BEES.

M. Gaston Bonnier, in a communication to the Academie des Sciences, has made some interest- ing observations on the habits of bees. In the afternoons, when they are, collecting water on the leaves of acoustic plants, he points out, they will not touch honey offered to them on these leaves, or on floats of various colours. But if honey is offered to them in the morning in a similar way it is carried off. M. Bonnier ex- plains this as arising from the strictness with which bees obey orders. If they are sent out for water, they will not stay to gather honey.

div.head: FUSING REFRACTORY METALS.
div.p: FUSING REFRACTORY METALS.

Professor Henri Moissan, the distinguished isolater of fluorine, and pioneer in the produc- tion of artificial diamonds, has been continuing his important experiments on the fusion and volatilisation of the.. more refractory metals in the electric furnace. He finds that in this fur- nace platinum, which only melts at a tempera- ture of over 3,200 deg. F., distils as easily as water does on an ordinary fire. Of the metals usually associated with platinum in nature, os- mium, palladium, iridium, and rhodium, Profes- sor Moissan found palladium to be the most easily fusible. And it is interesting to note that of these metals palladium has the smallest atomic weight except rhodium.

div.head: ARTIFICIAL BREAD AND MEAT.
div.p: ARTIFICIAL BREAD AND MEAT.

A glimpse into a field of vast possibilities has been given at Berlin by Dr. Emil Fischer. The work of the chemist has brought into prominence the amino-acids, and these Dr. Fischer pro- nounces the milestones on the road to artificial albumen our most essential food element. When the amino-acids are freed from water, the anhydrides greatly resemble peptones, a group of bodies occurring in the stomach. of all ani- mals, and not one of which has yet been arti- ficially produced. Peptones result from the de- composition of albumen by the ferments of the pancreatic glands, this decomposition being the process known as digestion. Albumen being the principal constituent of all animals and of grain, its artificial production means artificial food— both broad and meat.

div.head: HUMAN BODY AS TRANSMITTER.
div.p: HUMAN BODY AS TRANSMITTER.

An interesting feature of an electrical exhibi- tion held at the Madison-square Gardens, New York, was the demonstration that the human body may be used as a wireless telegraph trans- mitter or receiver. Professor Ovington, of Bos- ton, was the demonstrator, and he used the body of his assistant as radiator instead of the usual mast in sending wireless meesages. The human mast standing on an elevation held a wire from the electrical machine in one hand, while the other was raised aloft. The currents from the machine, which was operated in the usual way, radiated as wireless waves from his body. The messages were received by the usual wire an- tenna. High frequency currents of 200,000 volts were thus sent through the Amman bodyi

div.head: ARTIFICIAL PROTOPLASM:
div.p: ARTIFICIAL PROTOPLASM:

------- - -- Artificial protoplasm was discovered a few years ago, when two German scientific men found that a minute drop of a mixture of oil and a salt of potash acted like a microscopic living thing in several ways. It would rnoTe about spontaneously, change its form, had a circulatien in itaelf, would gather to itself par- ticles of other matter in its neighbourhood, and was sensitive to stimulus from the outside. Thus the material was called artificial protoplasm. It comported itself like a thing of life in all ways but one—it could not reproduce its like. The work is still being investigated, with the hypo- thesis that if the proper chemical constituents can be found and added it will then be a real artificial living thing. It already possesses four out of the five distinguishing characteristics of a living thing.

WONDERFUL NEW SEARCHLIGFIT. A Consul at Geneva write': At Cain, on the Lake 'of Geneva, at an altitude of 3,600 feet, there has been submitted to the officers of the Swiss general staff a new searchlight. It is re- ported as having been a success, at the search- light was handled with the greatest ease, mend- ing its powerful rays a distance of seven and a- half miles. Objects at six and a-half miles could be distinctly seen. The machine providing the power was a twenty-four horse-power and fur- nished 1,000,000 electric candle-power light. A forty horse-power motor would give 12,000,000 electric candle-power. The great advantage of this searehligkt is that it may be elec- trically handled in all directions by wire from a distance of 656 feet from the motor oar, which transports it and sends it to the required spot. It thus enables the driver and observer to send the rays to any place they desire without being blinded by the light, and places them under shelter from the enemy's sm.

div.head: DISUSE OF THE BRAIN.
div.p: DISUSE OF THE BRAIN.

--- - A well-known medical authority warns people of the dangers to health from indolence and dis- use of the brain. The medical profession cannot too strongly insist upon some sort of occupation to keep the brain in waive use: Many 'pereons have worked too hard, and worn themselves out at an early age. Elderly persons, and oven those of middle age, havin given up business and professional life, and having laid aside their vocations without having other interests or pur- suits to which to turn, may become plunged into destondency or premature dotage. All great brain workers have lived to an advanced age. Ile had seen several cases of mental disease in- duced solely by enforced idleness in -men who had been turned out of public service or had given up their busineeit too, early in life. 'lt would be better to arrange gradual oeosation of work and not break off horn sudden hard work to idleness. Persons, too, who belong to the w- eaned "leisured elan," unless pursuing some hobby, soon show signs of brain diens..

HOW TO GET NEW RUBEER FOR OLD. A process for regeneratin old rubber has for its principle the separation of the caoutchotto proper oontained in vulcanised rubber from the mineral and other matters which have been in- corporated into it, such as sulphur, &c. The first operation consists in dissolving the vul- canised rubber in one of the usual solvents, using petroleum preferably either alone or with ben- zine added to it. After treating for a, certain time the insoluble matter is separated by filter- ing under pressure, or by a centrifugal machine. The solution when separated from the insoluble matter is evaporated to the consistence of syrup finder a reduced pressure, and is then taken up by acetone. The liquid which is thus obtained is first boiled and then decanted off, and The rubber is again taken up by an alcoholic soda solution. After boiling and pouring off a second time, the rubber is treated with boiling alcohol. After the alcohol is taken off, the rubber is washed with water and then dried by super- heated steam, which removes the last traoe of alcohol and water it my contain.

div.head: FLUID LENSES.
div.p: FLUID LENSES.
, I

A report f;o7n---onsul-General Rublee, at Vienna, states that after experiments extending over a number of years a Hungarian chemist has succeeded in producing optical lenses by a simple and cheap process, that arc not only quite as good as the best massive glass lenses at prosent used, but that can be manufactured of a ,size three times as great as the largest homo- geneous glass lens heretofore made. The lens consists of a fluid substance enclosed between two unusually hard glass surfaces similar to watch crystals, in which the refractive power and other characteristic properties are so chosen that the glass surfaces not only serve to hold the fluid, but also combine with the fluid to over- come such defects as are scarcely to be avoided in ordinary lenses. It is for this reason also that the lens is achromatic.

The fluid contained in the lens is hermetically sealed, so that no air can enter and exercise a damaging effect. The fluid does not evaporate, and its composition is such that its properties are not affected by time or by temperature. The ooefficient of expansion, both of the glass and of the fluid, is approximately the same be- tween the temperatures of 15deg. of cold to 66derr. of heat. Another advantage of the len= tnat on account or tile tact that toe num is net dense and the glass crystals are thin, the whole lens combination through which the Light must penetrate is very slight.

ME DEAR CHILDREN,— 'P As July is here, I expect you are all look- ing forward with a large amount of pleasure to your approaching holidays. This summer weather is delicious, especially if one is fortu- nate enough to live by the sea or in the coun- try. I wonder what you will do when the schools break up, and you are free to roam about all day without a care of lessone. I, re- member how pleased I used to be when the holidays came round, and I was free to go fishing and butterfly hunting. Well, that is all over now for me, but I am equally pleased to hear how you all amuse yourselves. I am sure many of you like school; but, if you did not have an occasional break, it would become very weary. I am awarding a prize this week to Gladys Knight, who sent me the first correct solutions to puzzles; also a prize to Margery Frockley for her story. I hope next week to be able to announce the winners cf the last monthly comrstition for t, oys and girls. It strikes me Ishall have quite a difficulty lodecide the first prize winner for the pincushions, they all look so pretty. The boys, too, have evi- dently been trying their best with the essay. I am sure you will all enjoy reading the piece of poetry sent me by Lily Blackford and Lucy Fitzpatrick. I only wish I could award you all prizes, but I find that those who persevere eventually succeed in being rewarded.—With all good wishes from

div.head: GERALD'S GARDEN.
div.p: GERALD'S GARDEN.

It was a sunny afternoon in March. Gerald was in the garden digging, with tiny epade, and his mother was looking at him. Then she took him to a sunny corner in the garden, and told him he might call that part his own, to dig in just as he liked. At that he dug away busily, then he walked round the garden, with his little spade on his shoulder, just as he had seen the gardener do. There were some tiny plants peeping out of the ground, and Gerald liked the look of the fresh new green, so he began to dig them up and carry them to his own garden, but he did not know how to plant them. The' nest day, when mamma walked round the gar- den, ehe could not find her nice little plants; but, when she got to Gerald's garden, there they lay, looking very sadly indeed. Mamma called the gardener, and told him to take them back to where they cam. from. Gerald cried very loudly, for he did not like them to be touched. But Gerald had to learn not to touch what did not belong to him.
BARRY E. CLARKE.

Those who love Nature at her wildest might do worse than select the North Riding of Yorkshire for a wheel holiday. The district from the vale of Pickering northwards to Whitby and Middlesbrough is not overrun bytourists. In these wide stretches of moorland days may be spent on the heather with no sound but the buzz of the bee, and a delicious scent fills the air. The explorer is drawn into wild glens full of bracken, and he may wander for miles from dale to dale, corning upon old. mills and solitary farmhouses amidst romantic scenery. The Cycle Parade. Sir,—The Collectors' Committee earnestly appeals for assistance in the form of collectors on the occasion of the fancy dress parade and carnival, to be held in aid of the infirmary Extension Fund on July 21st, and in endeavourir.g to assist this necessary work for the relief of human suffering particularly begs the help of all superintendents of Sunday schools, warks' managers and others in the furtherance of this laudable object. They would be glad if all the Sunday school superin- tendents would make a special appeal to their teachers and acholars to act as collectors, and forward a list of those willing to assist in this manner to the under- signed not later than the Pith instant. Trusting a generous response will be made to this appeal. Yours faithfully,
GEORGE WALKER, (Chairman). J. J. PRITCEIARD, (Hon. Sec.) 3, Wellfleld-street, Warrington. "Trade Union Methods." 'No Good to the Painting Trade."

We are informed that the MS letter sent to us on the above topic in the name of" Walter 1 Pearce, lectuser at the Manchester Technical School " was not written by or sent to us by Mr. Pearce, and also that the signa- ture is a forgery. Mr. Pearce further points out that he is not, and has not been for several years, a lecturer at the _lanchester or any other Technical School, nor has he any official connection with the Manchester educational authorities As many of the expressions used in the letter are extracted from the published opinions of Ntr. Pearce,he desires to add, that whilst strongly disagreeing with some of the methods of trades unionism, especially in connection with the painting trade, he has been for 35 years, and still is, an active and consistent advocate of Trades unionism in its general principles ; a friend and comrade of many of its past pioneers,and a close student of its action and working upon the painting trade both here and on the Continent.

Beautiful Warrington Society. Sir,—As the beautiful weather and the time of year were the cause of but a moderate attendance at the annual meeting of this society,will you kindly give me a little of your valuable space to call attention to one or two matters of importance? That the influence of the society is making itself felt in the town I think every candid person will admit. To mention only one point,the number of window-boxes has greatly increased I and is already lending to the houses in our streets a brightness and beauty to whichbitherto they have been strangers. But there are two matters of importance on which I shall be glad to elicit the opinions of those interested in this work. First, is it possible to create a garden city suburb for Warrington? There is good hope of this being accomplished at Oldham, and if it can be done there, -why not here? We ought to have in the coming autumn some expert speaker on this subject, who would explain how this had been done in other places and how by the co-partnership in housing system, the tenant gradually becomes owner a his house. But, meanwhile, can we make people enthusiastic about the garden city? The pretty, well-built house, standing in his own garden : the ample recreation ground : the avenues of trees: the absence of ugliness and dirt—ls not something of this kind worth working for ? By you kind help, Sir, let us ventilate the idea and brace ourselves up to endure the cold water poured upon it. The second place upon which I invite criticism is the scheme which emanates from Philadelphia for dealing with waste places. There are in every town certain spots waiting for the builder. Sometimes they wait for years. The Philadelphian plan is to get the owner's permission to use these idle plots for allotments or gardens until they are required for building. By this means a good deal can be done to make "The desert 'blossom as the rose "and to beautify our towns. What do your readers think? I am, sir, your obedient servant,
MOR LEY STEVENSON.

The -Savage Suffragettes. am honoured by your taking notice of my letter of remonstrance against the leaderette you published a -fortnight ago. Seeing that you have thus far condes- cended, I must not complain, I suppose, of you applying the word" glibly "to nay remarks. It is scarcely cor- rect, though, but perhaps permissible under the circum- stances. An ordinary correspondent ought not to be so presumptuous as to protest against an Editor's edict. He deserves all that he gets—and more. You say that you "had not suspected that Miss Billington and many of her co-agitators possessed any reputation at all except the somewhat notorious .cue Testiltant from disturbing public meetings and fighting the police." You never heard of her before. Of course not. She was only an ordinary woman, acting as •organizer for the Independent Labour Party, wlio made no pretence at anything beyond striving to elevate the masses. She did have the temerity, a few months ago, to debate with a Liberal M.P., and if you happen to come across the printed report you will see that she more than held her own. In fact, the same individual ismovv considering the error of his ways, for he has joined the Socialist movement. You evidently know Lady Carlisle better. She is an educated person and, of course, she has a title. Fancy, however, her ladyship saying that the suffragettes are "‘ making an important mockery of womanhood." Even , Lady Carlisle is net particular as to the choice of her adjectives. " Important mockery !" . . . What does the Lady mean by ." an important mockery ?" Is it a delicate, lady-like way of expressing "sympathy," ' or is it another of those " inexactitudes we have heard so much about recently ? " Fighting the police." That is a dreadful sin. What you object to, apparently, is not that the ladies should have votes but that votes should be given only to those ladies Who know how to behave themselves. Suppose, for instance, that we were to apply the same restriction so as to effect" mere man." How many individuals would have votes at election times ? Further, take typical case—the Right Hon. John Burns, M.P. Would John Burns, do you think, be in the Cabinet to-day if ,he had not also been put in prison for obstruction and "utigentlesiarrliness," so called? Was he not denounced at one time, by respectable law-abiding citizens? If it had not been fbr his zeal in the cause he once had so so much at heart, and -for his contempt for " man-made law," you would not be called upon, from time to time, to sing his praises so lustily. Experience is a valuable instructorand we may derive an important advantage from taking notice of events that have happened. -These ladies may be wrong in endeavouring to assert themselves. They would, doubtless, have pleased the quiet, unassuming, lady-like upholders of womanly dignity if they had been content to remain at home, submitting themelves to their lords and masters, smothering their ideals in nain and solitude, and bringing rip their children in the same servile way. They have far more courage than that, and, what is more, they are not afraid of sacrificing themselves for their poorer sisters. It may be considered, by some, to be below the dignity of womauhoo.-1 to plead for others. It may be rude far a lady to argue with a gentleman on matters political. It mar be that poverty is considered a crime now-a-days. There cannot, however, be any exam for a gentleman (or a lady either') to accuse some women of want of tender- ness, or of graceful attention, or of being refined and virtuous, or less beautiful or loveable. because they are burning with a passion to submit themselves than manner of harsh treatment so lons as their sex may someday be treated equitably. If they bequeath to the rising generation what they are now sacrificing themselves for—votes for women—their arguments, will be forgotten but their names will berevered.—Yonrs trnly, EDMUND OSBORN'E. '29, Lovely-lane, Warrington, 4th July, 1506.

CROSFIELD'S FIRE BRIGADE. An Up-to-date Station. The handsome new tire engine station at the works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfleld and Sons Limited, has been completed this week and it may safely be said that the building is one of the !best of its kind in the country. It provides the most ample accommodation and is replete with all the up-to-date fire fighting appliances, while architecturally it is quite in keeping with the imposing block of buildings which contain the recently- opened general °aces. Thanks to the graft interest which the firm has taken in the fire brigade the men have attained the highest state of efficiency and we believe that an independent expert has given it as his opinion that this is the best equipped and most efficient works tire service in the Kingdom. The man brigade consists of 50 men, selected with regard to the nearness of their homes as well as to their personal fitness for fire brigade duties. Eight of these are organised as a team of Pompiers and are skilled in the use of the "Hook and Ladder" system : they carry pomnier hooks on their belts even in ordinary escape drill. In addition to these, eight men are attached to the brigade as fire police. Of the 50 men in the main brigade. 24 are on the active list and the rest on the reserve. The latter come up for training 12 times in the year and 10 of them are passing through a course of instruction. As these become efficient they give way to others and thus an auxiliary force of some eighty men has been built up, available for emergencies. With regard to the new building, the machine room lon the ground floor is 70 feet long and 40 feet wide, and the height is 14 feet. The floor is laid with adamantine tiles, end the walls are handsomely tiled lin two shades of green. There is an effective freize 2 lfeet deep. Four modern automatic-opening doors form a striking feature. By pulling a handle at the back of the station the doors may be instantly opened, either separately or simultaneously. The door by which the fleemen enter from the works also opens automatically as soon as the bolts are realized, and immediately on entering the firemen see a large indicator screen. This enables them at a, glands to locate the position of any outbreak in the works, and to tell which machines are required. There is also a system of duty checks so Ithat the fireman, by noting which checks have already been removed from the screen when he arrives, is at i once acquainted with the nature of the duty he s ex- pected to perform. The screen is also furnished with telephones connected Teith the general system and also with the firemen's dwellings. The, lighting arrange- ments are very complete. They have been carried out by the staff of the firm and include electricity and gas installations. The fire-tighting. apparatus which is housed in the machine room is of the most modern description and includrs two steamers, two escapes and automatic harness. In addition there are a number of special appliances, largely of the firm's own invention or design. On hooks affixed to the walls hang the firemen's uniforms and accoutrements, and it should be noted , that each man is provided with two full sets of uniform. I The firemen have formed themselves into a self-support- ing club for social, intellectual and physical recreation, and weekly meetings are held. The second stores- of the new building will serve the useful pnrposea of the firemen's recreation room and the girls' dining-room, and it is admirably adapted for use in these ways. On the roof of the structure is an entirely new departure in the shape of a garden which, it is expected, will in time be a place of beauty amid a scene of industry. In addi- tion to the departments already named, the station includes a store room and a dentist's room. The able superintendent of the tire brigade, which has aequitted itself with great credit in various competi- tions, is Mr. Gallon.

div.head: CHILDREN'S BREAKFAST.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S BREAKFAST.

--- The children's breakfast is often hurried, or the little ones are perhaps fretful and have no appetite, or do not fancy it. As often es not they go to school without n proper meal, and their brains are consequently unable to perform the tasks set them. Anxious mothers should take to heart the advice of the King's physician, Sir Francis Laking, and give their children plenty of currant bread.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
SIR HENRY HIBBERT DISTRIBUTES THE PRIZES.
The Improved Position of the Teaching Profession.

There was a large attendance at the annual prize- giving in connection with the Warrington Training College which took place on Saturday afternoon. As usual considerable interest centred in the proceedings, the audience including many of the relatives and friends of the students. Sir Henry Hibbert, chairman of the Education Committee of the Lanca- shire County Council, presided and distributed the prizes. He was supported on the platform by the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson (prineipal), Ven. Archdeacon Sponer (hon. secretary to the College Committee), Rev. Canons Kelly and Willis, Rev. H. B. Blogg, Lieut. Col. Buckton, Mr. W. S. Kinch; the mem- bers of the Resident Staff and second and first year students. The following accepted the Principal's invita- tion to be present :—Lady Hibbert and Miss Hibbert, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Blogg, Mrs. Buckton,Mr. E. M. Hance (Director to the Liverpool Education Council), Mr. 0. Duthie (director to the Salford Education Council) Mr. J. Moore Murray (director to the Warrington Education Committee) and Mrs. Moore Murray, Mr. T. W. Broivnwell (inspector to the Manchester Educa- tion Council) and Mrs. Brownvvell, Rev. F. W. E. Chadwick, Rev. H. B. Firth, Rev. H. A. and Mrs. Lester, Rev. B. and Mrs. Percival, Rev. W. and Mrs. Pollock. Hill, Rev. T. A. J. Ridpath, Rev. N. Wilson, Mr. CH White, Dr. and Mrs. Adams, Dr. and Mrs. Bowden, Dr. I Lee (Liverpool), Dr. and Mrs. Guest Gornall, Dr. and Mrs. Joseph, Mr. and Mrs. R. H. Jovnson. Alderman and Mrs. A. Bennett, Misses Adams, Miss Barker, Miss Beardmore, Mr. Mrs. and Miss Blair, Mr. Mrs. and Miss Alice Ringers, Mr. and Mrs. G. W. A... Brown, Mr. end Mrs. Carruthers, Mrs. .7. and the Misses Davies, Mrs. and Miss Fairclough, Miss F. Perry, Miss Rhodes, Mr. Robson, Mr. and Mrs. Rossiter, Mr. and Mrs.Ruddock, Mrs. and Miss Rvlands, Miss Shaw, Mrs. Singleton, Miss Taylor, Miss M. Timewell, the Misses Watkins. the Misses White, the Misses Willis (Halsnead Park) Mr. and Mrs. H. Woods, Mr. and Mrs. Sc. S. Woods, Mrs. Asbridge, Miss Bassnett. Mr. Bentley. Mrs. Brittain, Mrs. Caton, Mrs. Clark, Mr. and Mrs. Christopher, Miss Crawford, Mr. F. and Miss M. Cres- well, Mr. Crompton, Mr. and Mrs. A. DeinnSey. Miss May Durbin, Mr. and Mrs. Edgar, Mrs. England. Mrs. Feber, Miss Fisbwick,Mr. and Mrs. Freeman,Mr. Gooch. Miss Hall, Mrs. Hamilton, Miss B. Haythornthwaite, Mr. Higson, Mrs. Hill. Mrs. Holland, Mr. Holnie' Mr. and Mrs. Houghton. Mrs. Howard, Mrs. Hudson, Mrs. Hughes, Mrs. Jenks, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Kelly, Mrs. Lawrenson, Mrs. Lidiard, Mrs. Lightfoot, Mrs. Lovell, Mrs. Lowthian, Miss Lowthian. Mrs Lloyd, Mrs. McDowell. Miss Martins Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Newton, Mr. Parke, Miss Pownall, Mrs. Saint, Mrs; Shaw, Miss Slater, Miss Stevenson. Miss Stott, Mr. Swift, Mrs. Taylor, Mrs. Tayler, Mrs. and 'Miss Thompson, Miss Tuke, Mrs. Turner, Miss Walker. Mrs. Webb, Mrs. Winterbottom, Mrs. Wright, Mrs. Wyer. The PRINCIPAL said that was the twenty-second time he had opened the proceedings at the annual prize giving, and he was sure they would sympathise with him in the extreme difficulty of finding something different to say. (Laughter.) After intimating that he would refrain from alluding to the Education Bill— a subject on which nearly every one had something to say—Canon Stevenson said therewasonething he would like to say a few words about. They had to face a new state of things in regard to the future teachers of the country. A very large number of them were taking up their profession without passing through the training colleges. This was largely the result of one of those changes which the Board of 'Education occasionally made and slipped into the code without saying much about it. It seemed an innocent thing at the time, and it was only when they saw what was the result that they found out the evil. The Board of Educa- tion had very materially lowered the standard of the examination which was passed by those ' who did not pass through a Training College, and consequently the examination which his students ! were going to pass next week—(leughter)—and any reference to which always raised in their minds a pleasurable sense of anticipation—(laughter)—was of a very much more severe character than the examination to be undergone by those who did not enter a college but simply sat for their certificates outside. The result was that a large number of people, beginning to find out that the external examination was very much easier than the internal, said to themselves : " Why should T have the expense of going to college? Why should I have to give up those two years? Why should not I continue to act as an assistant teacher in the school and peas this very easy examination and so qualify myself for my profession ?" He was happy to say that the education authorities, at all events the large ones, were beginning to find this out and already one or two of them hod made considerable alterations in their scales of salaries by which they recognized that the trained teacher ought to be remunerated at a considerably higher rate than the untrained teacher. (Applause.) That, of course, bad yet to make its way, and at the present moment it was a great disapnointrnent to many of them to see the very large number of yonne people who deliberately refrained from attempting to enter a training college.Tt was not merely a question of examinations or of the amount of knowledge which a, person received.. He honestly believed that the gain of the college course to the young people themselves—a gain which was not te be measured by any examinations passed or successes achieved—the gain of two years of uninterrupted study under the guidance of experienced persons, of meeting and learning to know each other, of having their angles rubbed, off by contact with other people, of the refine- ment which must come from the various educational and other privileges to be found within the walls of the college—all these things contributed to the intellectual and aesthetic and also to the moral culture of the young teacher in a way which no amount of study at home and passing examinations in one's own town could possibly contribute. He earnestly honed it would go forth from that meeting that if the teachers of the future were to ' be what they wished them to be, it was indispensable I that they should have some such years of education as were provided for them in the training colleges. With regard to the work of the past year. they had received a very remarkable distinction in the subject in which they least expected to receive it—physical instruction or drill. The students had submitted themselves to an examination conducted by a gentleman who was in the habit of examining for many training colleges and the I 'mein educational authorities of the kingdom end whose I certificate prinked as one which it was desirable far the teacher to obtain. He (the Principal) had received a report from the examiner which was so good that he °mild hardly believe it to be true. (Laughter.) He said- that of all the colleges he had examined he had never found one in which the students so thoroughly knew their work in that subject as they did in the War- rington College. (Applause.) Then, going quite to the other sad of the scale, they had just received the results of the examination in religious knowledge and the list was the best they had ever obtained since the college was founded. (Applause.) The whole of the second year stmients. with the exception of three, were Placed in the first class, and those three passed second. Therefore they would see that spiritually, if he might so put it, as well as nhv3ically the students had every reason to congratulate themselves. (Laughter find applause.) Canon Stevenson then made a feeling refer- ence to the death of Dean Manhire. of Manchester. who was for eighteen years secretary of the college and took the deepest interest in its :teal fare. He (Canon Steven- son) had always found him the kindest, wisest, end most expert of counsellors and what the loss to the college, to the committee, and to himself had been, it was quite impossible for him to say. He was happy to announce that they had in Dean Maclure's successor— Archdeacon Spanner—(applanse)—one in regard to whom they could feel that if such an irreparable lose had to be sustained the vacant place con'd not he better filled then it had been. Canon Stevenson cencluderl by welcoming Sir Henry Hibbert and referring to his greet experience of erluentional work se chairman of the Lancashire County Education CoMraittee.

Sir HENRY HIBBERT, who was cordially received, slid his first words *mist be congratulatory to the students whose magnificent work he had seen upstairs. He took a great deal of interest in art training. And he was free to confess that he had never seen a better example of blackboard drawing than the one on view that afternoon. (App%llse.). If Canon Stevenson felt a difficulty in finding something new to Say what must his,(Sir Henry's) position he when that was the llgth speech he had made on education since the Bill came into operation 1n1902 ? (Laughter and Applause). Whatever else he said, he would keen clear of the denominational aspects of the Bill of 190 g. He ' had had an extremely difficult task during the last three or four veers as chairman of a committee embracing all shades of political and reliTious belief in the adminis- tration of education probably in the most difficult educa- tional area in England and Wales. Tt was, however, his proud boast that they had never had the slightest fric- tion from the appointed day to the present time. (Applause). A great deal had been said shout the sufficiency of raining college accommodation, Be admitted that probably up to the last two or three years there had been sufficient accom- modation for those who cared to take advantage of it. Tint they now wanted to look at the questioo from an entirely different point of view. Whatever might be the merits or demerits of the Act of 1902 it had had the effect of improving the position of the teacher. It had raised the profession and had given the autho- rities the means of embarking on systems of secondary education which ultimately would he of advantage not only to the teaching profession but also to the nation. In the Lancashire Education Committee's area they were giving £lO,OOO per annum more to the same teachers than they received in 1902. In addition they

were lightening the labours of those teachers by increas- ing the staffs to the extent of another £40,000 per aniitim. The total increased expenditure on the staffing of the schools since 1902 approximated very closely on £lOO,OOO per annum. While they had been careful in looking after the material prosperity of the teachers, he was bound to say in defence of his committee and similar committees that they had not lost sight of that safeguarding of the interests of the ratepayers which ought to be one of the things which a public man considered. They, how- ever, felt that the teaching profession—one of the noblest in which a man or woman could engage—was inadequately remunerated : hence the increase. And what would be the effect of this? What profession was therein which a woman could embark, where she would be so well paid and where herpaolidays would be greater than those given to any profession in the world ? The teaching profession under the new and altered conditions held out such inducements that the authorities not only expected to get more teachers but they hoped to get teachers of a better:calibre;and trusted that people would not be so foolish in the future when they were unable to make provision for their girls, as to send them out as governesses with the salaries of third-rate cooks, when they could be occupied in so remunerative a manner as teaching in the elementary schools. (Applause). They were taking the first step in the direction of improving the material for their teaching staffs, by endeavouring to educate side by side those girls who were intending to belong to the profession, and those whose parents were in the happ, position of allowing them to have no profession at all. They hoped by that means to rub off the corners. They wanted a greater community of interest; they wanted to create an atmosphere. The Secondary school system of this country was undergoing a great change, and there were bound to be hundreds and thousands of remunerative positions for the best girls of the class who were now in the training colleges. It all depended upon the students I themselves. Girls who left a college of that ' description ought not to be satisfied simply with a certificate. They ought to have an even higher ambition, and although it was perfectly true that the students who came to that college were primarily trained for the elementarysehools,still there was a very great want in the seconciadischools of teachers who had been taught how ta teach. (Applause). Continuing Sir Henry pointed out that of 4,290 teachers in the Lancashire County area, only 1;623 were certificated, 1,358 were uncertificated, 598 were supplementary teachers, and 705 were pupil teachers. Influenced no doubt by theory of the ratepayers, they in that area were not staffing their schools as they ought to do. He was one of those people who believed that one could get accustomed to paying rates. (Laughter.) He was , perfectly certain that every day the popularity of education grew. Although at the moment 4r3 per cent. only of their teachers were certificated, he felt sure that the percentage I would increase rapidly, thus finding occupation for the girls whose fathers and mothers had the good sense to I give them the immeasurable advantage of a training college education. (Applause). In giving advice to the students, Sir Henry appealed to them not to teach merely to get a living. He knew everyone had to live and in one way or another everyone had to work. But /teaching to get a living ought not to be the be all and end all of their lives. There was a moral and material side of their education. They must be careful of the example they set their students. "Do not" said Sir Henry" be frightened of yourselves and do not be always looking at the clock to see whether it is twelve o'clock" I (Laughter). Continuing Sir Henry said that in some of the congested districts the teacher was the only lady with whom many of her little charges came in contact and it entirely depended upon her how they appraised the name "lady." He asked the students not to be always striving for more holidays. There was a maximum to the patience of those who had to pay for the holidays—when the holidays were constantly increasing in the schools. Those who had the conduct of public affairs wanted the teachers to have good salaries and an abundance of recreation, but there was a maximum, and he asked them not to over- step it. Sir Henry concluded by quoting the words of Kingsley : "Take pains, take trouble. Whatever you do, do 1 thoroughly. Whatever you begin, finish. It may not seem worth your while at the moment to be so very painstaking, so very exact. In after years you will find it was worth your while, that it has paid you by—training your character and soul,paid you by giving you success in Ii fe,paid 'you by giving you the respect and praise of your fellow-men, paid you by helping you towards a good conscience and enabling you in old age to turn back and say" I have been of use upon earth." (Applause).

div.head: PRIZES.
div.p: THE PRIZES.

Sir HENRY HERBERT then distributed the prizes as follows :—Adelaide Shaw, Marie Newton, and Marion Lowthinn, divinity ; Alice Christopher and.. Margaret Edgar, highest marks in all subjects (first prize) ; May Houghton, highest marks in all subjects (second prize); Ruth Asbridge, practical teaching (girls) ; Annie Forrester, practical teaching (infants) ; May Houghton, principles of teaching ; Alice Christopher, arithmettc and algebra; Margaret Edgar, euclid ; Margaret Edgar and May Houghton, literature Margaret Edgar and May Houghton, literature : May Houghton, literature essay ' • Agnes Freeman. English composition and French ; May Houghton, the hest letter ; Annie Forrester, reading and recittaion •, Margaret Edger. history and geography; Elizabeth I Thompson, history essay ; Annie Forrester and 1 Agnes Freeman, practical science • Alice Christopher and May Houghton, nature study; 'Eugenie Cresswell, needlework ;,Alice Christopher, drawing (bookwork) ; Margaret Dempsey, drawing (blackboalrd) .; Hannah Fawcett, theory and practice of music. C.anon KELLY mooed a vote of thanks to Sir Henry Hibbert and referred with satisfaction to the improved position of the teaching profession. There was a time when it did not receive that respect to which it was entitled and which it was receiving to-day. It was a matter for rejoicing, that the education question had in the various boroughs and country districts brought together men of different views, all animated by the sincere desire to promote the well-being of the country at large. There was, continued the speaker, always a danger lest they should make their anxiety not to be called upon to expend any more than they were obliged, so predominant in their minds as to drive away the higher thought of how the education of the country was to be carried on. They could not do the work without expenditure. What they had to see was that the expenditure should not be lavish, but adequate to the deserts of those who were to receive it, and that it should be wisely administered. He would be sorry if there was any relaxation of the efforts which were being made to put England in the forefront in educa- tion. (Applause.) Canon Kelly made a sympathetic reference to the late Dean IWacluro with whom he was associated in his school and university days. Mr. Knccu seconded and Archdeacon SPOONER _sup- ported the motion, whice was heartily agreed to, and the meeting ended. Dnrine the afternoon the visitors inspected an interesting vhibition of needlework and drawing, which was highly creditable to the students. Tea was nerved in the College, and the Volunteer Band played selec- tions on the lawn.

div.head: REDUCING LOCAL LICENCES. The Assessing of Compensation. CAN BREWERS' PROFITS BE CONSIDERED P
div.p: REDUCING LOCAL LICENCES. The Assessing of Compensation. CAN BREWERS' PROFITS BE CONSIDERED P

An important point—whether brewers' profits can be considered in assessing compensation for suppressed licences—is being decided, and reference was made to the subject at the Warrington Police Court on Thurs- day. A meeting of the Warrington Compensation Authority vas held to consider the amounts of compensation payable in respect of the following licences :—Rope and Anchor, Buttermarket-street, owners, Greenall Whitley and Co., tenant, Wm. Donworth ; Queen's Hotel,- Sankey street, owners, the Corporation, tenant Richard Sanson ; Boar's Head, Pig Hill, persons inter- ested in compensation question, Messrs. Peter Walker and Son. Limited, Mrs. Bessie Fraser, Liverpool, and Alfred Wood (the latter being the tenant). Mr. Browne appeared for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.; Mr. A. T. Holloway (deputy town clerk) for the Corporation ; Mr. J. Longland for Mr. Sanson ; Mr. J. W. Knowles for Mrs. Fraser and Mr. C. H. Unsworth (on behalf of Mr. T. S. Steel) for Messrs Peter Walker and Son, Limited.

The magistrates on the bench were :—Mr. John Fair- dough (presiding), Aldermen,Smethorst. Francomb and Tinnion, Dr. Fox, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. S. Wright, C. White, J. Geddes, G. Pilling, and C. Jackson Holmes.

Mr. Browne said that in the matter of the Rope and Anchor,his instructions were to apply for an adjournment On May 30th and 31st a very important case was heard in the King's Bench division. The law provided that if the owners and tenants were not satisfied with the amount assessed by the magistrates they could go to the Inland Revenue Commissioners. In this case there was a dispute—as in a large number of others—as to whether the Commissioners were entitled to take into account brewers' profits. The Commissioners said they were not entitled to coasider them but only the value of the property with and without the licence. The amount claimed by the owners and tenants was £2,837 and the Inland Revenue authorities only assessed it at £455. It was clearly shown that this latter sum was absurd. Mr. Justice Kennedy reserved his decision and it had not yet been given. Therefore the Inland Revenue Commissioners were not in a position in any case where brewers' profits were claimed to make any assessment. In Liverpool and other places the Com- pensation authorities had adjourned their proceedings in consequence. If the Commissioners did not, know whether they were allowed to assess or not- their worships would be in an even more difficult position to adjudicate on the amount until the judgment was given In the case of the Rope and Anchor they had agreed as to the amount between the tenants and brewers, and of course in that sum were included brewers' profits. These naturally made a great difference, as in'the case pending decision by Justice Kennedy where £2,830 was claimed, the sum without the brewers' profits would be £1,538. He strongly urged the Bench in the interests of all parties to adjourn the CASe. Mr. Knowles thought the only course to take was to adjourn. He had not. added Mr. Knowles, thought that Messrs. Walker had a claim in the case of the Boar's Head.
Mr. Unsworth, on -behalf of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd., said he was instructed to ask for a month's adjournment. After discussion the Bench adjourned all the cases until September oth.

div.head: Open Air Service
div.p: Open Air Service

A successful open air service arranged by the Free Church Council was held on Sunday evening in Thelwall lane, Latchford. There was a very good attendance. The Rev. J. F. Matthews conducted, and Rev. W. Mellor and Mr. Robert Henshall were the speakers. Miss Smith contributed a solo. Many people came to their front doors and joined in the singing from hymm books provided.

div.head: Spiritual Principles of Nonconformity
div.p: The Spiritual Principles of Nonconformity

1 Rev. J. F. Matthews and the Education Question. The Rev. J. F. Matthews, of Latchford Baptist Church, spoke at the summer meeting of the Bolton and District Evangelical Free Church Council, at Eger- ton, on Saturday last. Mr. Matthews took for his sub- ject, the " Spriritualprinciples of Nonconformity." He declared that during the past 50 years Noncon- formists had grown in outlook, in culture, in their attitude to social life generally, and in numbers. Their intellectual emancipation had synchronized with the abolition of tests at Oxford and Cambridge. Their thirst for knowledge had been fostered by the non-residential universities in London and the prnvinces. Their wider social horizon had arisen from the larger life which Christianity had com- pelled them to live. Nonconformity had always stood for something positive. Though the word contained a negative particle, the early Nonconformists who first wore the title were men of sound learning and profound piety. They had left the Church of England because they refused to conform to a State enactment. They quietly accepted the confiscation of their livings. A , rational view of human life, a free and healthy criti- cism of the Bible, and a high notion of the functions of ' the Church had helped Nonconformists to sound a deeper note. Their root principle lay in the spirituality of the Church. It was free and independent and autonomous. It knew no head but Jesus Christ, and acknowledged none. It recognized no interference by the State, and allowed none. That was their teaching. That was their glory. Nonconformists who debated the education question of 1370 stood there : but for the tact that they were sold by their friends, the great and bitter quarrel of to-day woeld have ended floe and thirty years ago. Now, however, a great number of Nonconformists were , clamouring for Bible teaching in the schools; were practically admitting the right of the St-to to interfere in matters of religion ; were denying. in act the very principle that liky at the basis of their existence as Nonconformists. Would it be any wonder if, when they had to tight the batt e of disestablishment, they found themselves b und with their hands behind them? They would be taunted, and rightly so, with inconsistency and insincerity. He (Mr. Mathews) had no wish to place any weapons in the hands of Anglicans, but he was not going to be silent because a large majority of his brethren differed from him on the matter. It appeared to him that they were afraid of the logical consequences of their own position; that they were afraid to face the soundness and beauty of their own fundamental truth. They sheltered themselves behind the cry of the danger to the State, and to the child himself, by the complete abolition of religious teaching front elementary schools, The position was absurd. It revealed their cowardice. He asked them to accept his warning, to take their own position seriously, and to maintain it inviolate. They had in the Free Church movement an organization that had spread itself like a vast network over the whole kingdom. Bible schools could easily be established if they were seriously in earnest about the religious training of the dill s He hoped they would never sacrifice their conviction to party loyalty. They were Nonconformists first. They must hold by the great spiritual function of the Church. They would then be safe whether their ministry was directed to the cleansing of the social life of the nation, or upholding of public righteousness, and when they struck a blow in any cause, it would be for a victory as sure as it would be triumphant.

Earlestown triumphed over Newton on Saturday and now head the West Lancashire League. Warrington are two points behind and it behoves them to put forth every effort if they are to secui.e the chpmpionship this season.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

So many people were out of town on pleasure bent on Saturday that there were comnaratively few local cricket matches. The Warrington team had a relaxation from League cricket and journeyed to picturesque Bowdon where they engaged in a friendly match. The result was not at all gratifying from the visiOrs' point of view. for Bowdon were vintorious by a margin of 33 with four wickets to spare. In justice to the Warring- tonians it must be said that their eleven was far from representative,E. A. Connor,A. Duckworth and Thewlis being among the absentees. A trial was given to , Turner, a promising young wicket keeper, who created a favourable imprersion when playing for the Castle , Rubber team in a Works Competition match.

Going to the wicket first, Warrington were dismissed for 116. The feature of the inniales was a fine display by T. Wright, who compiled G 9. He hit out cleverly. end was applauded for many splendid strokes. P. B. Hawtin was in good form, but unfortunately had to retire hurt when his innings had realized 14. T. bhwling gave the batsmen much trouble, and he captured 6 wickets for 31 runs.

Bowdon were in a scoring mood and ran up 149 for the loss of six wickets before the time limit expired. At one time it looked as if Warrington would have a chance, for Podmore easily bowled Frost and Voss when they had made 25 and 12 respectively. A pro- longed stand by S. E. Rigg and F. Church placed the

div.p: Bowling.

Owing to the numerous works trips there was prac- tically no local bowling last Saturday. The works competition will be resumed to-day when the follow- ing teams will meet : Whitecross No. 2 v. Fletchers No. 2. Rylauds N 0.4 v. Crosflelds No. 1. Rvlauds No. 2 v. London and North Western. Flerchers No. 1 v. C.L.C. Referee, Mr. E. Scott.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

The fine weather of last week-end was particularly acceptable to the members of the Warrington Cycling Club who had arranged a very enjoyable outing. Riding to Chester about fourteen members made their way to the pretty riverside resort of Farndon. They found comfortable quarters at the Raven Hotel and altogether had an excellent time. The various places or interest in the neighbourhood were visited and boating was indulged in. Warrington was reached on Sunday evening after an exceedingly pleasant holiday. There was a large muster for Tuesday evening's riu. to Cuerdley Cross and on arrival a bowling match was played with Widnes Cycling Club. Victory rested with the Widnesians by a large majority. The rest of the evening Was spent convivially.

To-day (Saturday), the club will be the guests of their esteemed president (Mr. John Naylor) at Beeston, Towers. The run to his picturesque retreat is one of the most delightful in Cheshire and Mr. Naylor's princely hospitality has many times been bestowed on, the Warrington wheelers who fully apreciate it.

div.head: WALKING DAY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.
A SUCCESSFUL CHILDREN'S FESTIVAL.

Walking Day was a day of unalloyed pleasure for the children of Warrington. Once more the town kept high holiday and on every hand was evidence of the desire to make the occasion full of happy remembrances for the Effie ones. Best of all, the weather was kind. Although once or twice during the morning threatening clouds gathered, there was no rain to spoil the processions and the pretty spectacles which were the reSult of so much careful and painstaking preparations were seep to advantage. The field festivities later in the day also passed off very happily. Not- withstanding a good spell of genial sunshine, there was a cold touch in the atmosphere but the afternoor was perfectly fine.A sharp shower early in the evening gave rise to gloomy forebodings, but fortunately 'it was of short duration, and the excellent sports pro." grammes which had been arranged were carried aii! with the greatest zest. Thousands of spectators witnessed the processio in which the gaily-dressed youngsters ficured o°. profldly. The lawn in front of the Town Hail was the meeting place of the thousand 4of Church of Englanci and 'Nonconformist scholars and when the various contingents, with children looking radiantly haPPY and bright banners fluttering in the breeze, had tak°°. their places, the effect was most pleasing. At V° o'clock the marshals (Councillor Craik and Mr. R. Fairclough) gave the signal for the Blue Coat Sch,

to lead the‘Way througlithe centre gate, and the schools followeld in quick succession. Each - headed by a band and there was a grand array banners and bannerettes. There were ye/-' original features but hero and there one or two ph._ - innovations were noticed. and received—due kultuiT:t tion. St. Peter's school had a very charming disPla.Tic: A number of little girls were daintily attired as maids with white dresses and purple sashes and hat?, and the effect was very picturesque. St. Luke school' also made a brave shoNi. Several girls carrie" wands surmounted with garlands, whilst others were tastefully costumed as gipsies with jingling tambourines. The procession included many lurries conveying smiling infants,and prettily decorated mail" carts were also a feature. Baskets of choice flowers were caitied by groups of little maidens dressed lii white. From the great crowds which lined the route it was evident that there was no waning of interest in the procession, and the decorations of the streets, although not lavish, showed the desire of the trades- people to share in the general rejoicings of children's day. The Roman Catholics presented a very striking pageant which, it was the general opinion, excelled all previous efforts. As the long lifie of colour threaded its way through the streets the scene presented 109 beautiful and imposing and the spectators gave vent to -their appreciation by applauding. The banners molt of them works of art —were the great feature of the procession. All of them served to emphasis' some phase of the belief of the Church. There was 3 magnificent series bearing representations of the Seven Sacraments, while other handsome banners depicted Our Lady and the Saints. One banner, which made no pretensions to the artistic, had not been seea before. On it appeared the watchword itt hold letters : "No Surrender. catholic Schools for Catholic Children." Here and there the eye of the onlooker was arrested by a glittering processional cross, generally followed by ' altar boys in surplices. The superb grouping of the scholars added much to the general effect. Infants were to be seen carrying pretty floral devices and gilt Crosses while nearlY the children wore distinctive sashes. A statue of the Madonna 'and Child in pure white was carried on a base covered with a rich profusion of lilies and the streamers were held by little maids dressed in white. Several other sacred statues were much admired. Tile spectacle was indeed charming in the extreme • and worthily upheld the reputation which the Roman Catholics have always enjoyed for the beauty of their pageantry. As usual the majority of the Nonconformist children went straight from their respective schools 'the station and -entrained for rural resorts where tbe, enjoyed themselves to the full. Wycliffe and Cock.- hedge Mission Schools proceeded to Dunham Hill, Golborn-street Baptists, to Lymm, Ebenezer Free Church, Buttermarket-street to the Twiggery Farm, Ebenezer Particular Baptists to High Legh, St.John'e to Brodsham, Cairo-street Unitarians to Walton,Bold• street Wesleyans to Lymm,Ellesmere-street and Silvel street Wesleyans to Helsby, Sankey Bridges We leans to Hood-lane; Burtonwood ; Working Men Mission to a field at Sankey, Friars-green and Brie street Independent Methodists to Padgate, Brick- New Mission to Orford, Latchford Primitive Meth( dists to Morris B, ook, Foster-street Gospel Hall f Orford, the Friends of the First Day School I Whitley, the Spiritualist Lyceum a to Mersey Vie' Frodsham, and the Ragged School to a *field 1 Grappenhall Heyss. Band Contest.

A great attraction in the evening was the annu:il quick-step band contest which brought togeo a large number of spectators, Scotland-road beii crowded. The bands commenced to play at 7.30, there were five entries for three prizes and two sil, medals for conductors of bands winning first and secoi prizes. Mr. Thompson, of the Alexandra Hot o.`Aciated as secretary, and Mr. Appleton, of Earlestoc as the judge, Result :-1, Crosfield's ; 2, Borough ; Pioneer.

The Examiner, Saturday, July 7, 1906. THE PROSECUTION .OF A SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS. COUNCILLOR. VOTE OF THANKS TO MR. LOUIS HEN SHALL. A Great Public Service." There was an echo of the recent prosecution of a Town Councillor at the monthly meeting of the War- rington Town Council held on Tuesday evening. Councillor Lord hai given notice to move " That this Council tenders its thanks to Mr. Louis Henshall for the great public service rendered by him in exposing an attempt by a late member of this Council to use his position on the Council to obtain personal financial benefit; and further desires to place on. record its appreciation of Mr. Henshall's conduct in coming forward notwithstanding the threat of legal proceedings and striking a blow at all who disregard the honour and integrity Of public life." The MAYOR: Mr. Henshall has been thanked already. A letter has been written to him by the deputy Town Clerk. His Worship then read the follow- ing correspondence :—" Town Clerk's Office, Warring- ton, 31st May,1906. Dear Mr. Henshall.—Rex v.Arthur Peacock.—l have pleasure in enclosing you P.O. for 14a. ad. to cover expenses herein. At the same time let I me tender to you the thanks of the Corporation for , your public spiritedness in coming forward and giving evidence in a case which could not be otherwise than I most unpleasant to you.—Youre faithfully, A. T. I HALLAWAY, deputy town clerk." "Runnymede, Belvoir-road, Stockton Heath, Warrington, lit June 11906. Dear Mr. Hallaway.—Rex v. Peacock.—l am I obliged for your letter. It is not my wish to accept expenses. Perhape_you will transfer the amount to the Police Poor Box. I appreciate your thanks. True this has been a distasteful task, but from the out- set I recognized I was, in loyalty to Alder- man Tinnion, bound to justify the statement made by him in the heat of a debate in the Council Chamber, and I think the letter I wrote to Alderman Tinnion and which is printed in the Investigation Com- mittee Proceedings shows the spirit regulating my conduct in these unfortunate proceedings. To yourself in particular and your staff in general, I owe thanks for the courtesies I have received in making an unpleasant duty as easy as possible.—Yours faithfully, L. Hinisri ALL." Councillor LORD said that with all respect to the Mayor it was due that a vote of thanks should be passed in that Council Chamber to Mr. Henshall. He did not wish to enlarge on this painful subject, because it was painful that one of their members should have been expelled from the Council. He moved that a resolution of thanks be tendered to Mr. Henshall on Councillor CUNVINGTON seconded. The MAYOR: I think Mr. Henshall has been thanked enough. It is not the usual thing in prosecutions. Councillor LORD: You never had a similar case, so there is no precedent. Councillor BALL said he thought the services of Mr. Henshall had been sufficiently acknowledged in Mr. Hallawav's letter. They as a Council were the highest and most representative body in the town and when they went out of their way to thank persons for work done they ought to see that they ware representing the ceneral body of feeling in the town. He believed the thanks of the Council should only be tendered for some signal act of service or after long years of patient and persistent services to the community. Neither of those conditions was fulfilled in the present instance. He believed the evidence of Mr. Henshall before the Investigation Committee had to be almost drawn from hint. Had they, any reason to think that his actions were being inspired by a high ideal of public service? He did not think one isolated act of publics service should entitle Mr. Henshall to the thanks of the Council as the controlling and governing body of a large community. The Council ought to have a greater dignity and reserve its thanks for occasions of higher service. He did not think the present instance was worthy of a formal vote of thanks on vellum. Councillor STOTT, as a member of the Investigation Committee, said that what Councillor Ball had said was perfectly true. They hied very great difficulty in per- suading Mr. Henshall to rive his statement of the con- versition between himself and Mr. Peacock. The Couticil had,however,passed votes of thanks recently for services which were perhaps of no more value than those rendered by Mr. Henshall and it placed one in a diffi- culty He agreed with Councillor Ball that the thanks of the Council ought only to be tendered for special services willingly and not compulsorily given. In the case of Mr. Henshall, however, he must confess that his statement, when he did decide to give it, was given in a plain and straightforward manner, and could not be shaken in any way. The danger was that the thanks of the Council would becodse too cheap and not be of the value that they deserved to be, if the Council were not careful in tendering their thanks as public representa- tives. The MAYOR: Since I have been Mayor I have signed votes of thanks several times when it has been against the grain to do so. I don't want any more of it, and I hope that if you pass this you will allow the Town Clerk to sign it. Councillor PEMBERTON said he agreed to some extent with what Councillors Ball and Stott had said, but he knew the great difficulty which existed in getting a man to come forward in cases like this. There was not one man in a thousand who would come forward, but when one did so be deserved the thanks of a public body. He knew of many cases that could have been brought before the Council and the courts of the r country if they could have got men to do what Mr. I Henshall hid done. Mr. Henshall was reluctant in the first place to come forward because the duty vvaa not a pleasant one. It was all right and easy for a man to talk to his neighbour, but no man liked to be put on his oath in a court. The MAYOR: He could not help it. • Councillor PEMBERTON : You could not compel him to go. The MicrOß : That is a matter of opinion. Councillor PEMBERTON : He could have said he knew nothing about it and was not going to say anything. There is no law in the country that could have dragged it out of him. While I agree with Councillor Ball that we should be careful how we give our thanks, this is a case where they ought to be tendered. We have given the thanks of the Council for very much less service. The voting resulted as follows : FOR THR RESOLUTION. AGAINST. A Lady's Ride to .York, Even in the hands of a member of the weaker sex the possibilities of the modern bicycle are indeed remarkable. A lady Cyclist recently rode from London to York in 21 hours dead, her stoppages when deducted from the time, reducing it to 16 hrs. 39 min. Although for 200 miles the lady bad to contend against a head wind, she knocked 11 hours off her time on a previous jaunt over Dick Ttirpin's.legendary course. In the days of the high machine and the solid .tyre many vain attempts were made by strong riders to encompass this journey inside 24 hours. To-day the record stands at 10 hrs. 19 min. A Novel Camping Scheme. The 'Daily Mail' lately outlined a novel varia- tion uf agipsy holiday scheme, in which a motor car takes the place cf a van, leaving a 'party of ten eycli,ts to rove at pleasure through the country, mil,nleit with impedimenta by day, and yet inde- plident of hotels or inns for their meitk and sleep- ing accommodation. The motor car, proceeding at a moderato pace, carries all the baggage, a urge tent, utensils and food. By pre-arrangement, when a suitable spot is reached, the car is stopped and meals are served. At night, a camp is pitched, bedding unpacked, supper cooked, and there you arc Assuming that ten cyclists formed the party, the entire cost of a week's holiday on this plan is worked Out to equal £2 13s. 6d. a bead.
